pages.t: AI Driven, Human Assisted
pages.h: AI driven, human assisted: the default just inverted
pages.d: For a decade the default was human driven, AI assisted. That order is inverting — and the part left to a person gets harder, not easier. What actually changes.
pages.b: AI Driven, Human Assisted AI practice AI driven, human assisted: the default just inverted For most of the last decade the sensible arrangement was obvious — a person did the work, and a model helped at the edges. That order is flipping. The model holds the plan now and the person holds the veto, and the half left to the human turns out to be the harder half. Here is what actually changed, the four jobs that stay with you, where the inversion is a bad idea, and how I run it in production. Published 21 August 2026 · 12 min read · by Krunalkumar Shah The old default, and why it worked Human driven, AI assisted was never a slogan anybody had to argue for. It was simply how the tools worked. Autocomplete finished the line you were already writing. The grammar checker flagged a sentence you had already composed. The model suggested a function body inside a file you had already structured, in a project you had already designed. You held the plan; the tool shaved seconds off the typing. That arrangement was safe for a reason worth naming out loud: the unit of delegation was small enough to check at a glance. If a suggestion was wrong, you saw it the second it appeared, in context, with everything around it still loaded in your head. The cost of a bad suggestion was one keystroke — reject, move on. Nobody ever needed a governance policy for autocomplete. It was also, quietly, a ceiling. A tool that only ever operates one line ahead of you can never save you more than the typing. The thinking, the sequencing, the twenty small decisions between "I need this" and "this works" — all of it stayed with the human, because there was no way to hand any of it over. What actually changed The popular story is that the models got smarter. That is true, and it is not the interesting part. The shift that matters is much narrower: the model started holding the sequence. Give a current system a goal instead of a sentence and it will decompose it, choose tools, run them, read what came back, notice that it was wrong, and try again — for twenty or fifty steps — before it hands you anything at all. That is a different job. It is not writing your next line. It is running the loop you used to run. And once the loop moves, the unit of delegation moves with it. You are no longer accepting a token. You are accepting an outcome , produced by a process you did not watch. The entire safety story of the old arrangement — I'll catch it if it's wrong, because I'm right here — quietly stops bein

pages.t: Automating Email Replies with n8n
pages.d: How I build email reply automations with n8n: the five-stage workflow, where AI helps, guardrails that prevent bad sends, and mistakes to avoid.
pages.b: Automating Email Replies with n8n Automation Automating email replies with n8n Replying to the same kinds of emails over and over is exactly the sort of work software should handle. I've built several of these systems for real clients — including my open-source CleverResponder builds for SmartLead and Instantly. Here's how I structure them, where AI genuinely helps, and the mistakes worth avoiding. Published 18 May 2026 · 5 min read · by Krunalkumar Shah Why n8n for this n8n is a workflow automation tool where you connect building blocks — triggers, logic, and actions — into a flow, without writing a whole application from scratch. For email reply automation it fits well for a few reasons: it talks to email and CRM services out of the box, it lets you drop in custom logic where you need it, and because you can self-host it, sensitive message content doesn't have to pass through a third-party black box. You get the speed of no-code with an escape hatch to real code when a step needs it. The anatomy of a reply-automation workflow However fancy it looks, almost every email automation I build follows the same five-stage skeleton. Understanding this shape matters more than any single node: Trigger — something starts the flow: a new reply lands in an inbox, or a campaign tool like SmartLead or Instantly fires a webhook. Fetch & parse — pull in the message and pull out what matters: sender, subject, body, and any context from a CRM about who this person is. Classify — decide what kind of message this is. Interested? Not interested? A question? Out of office? This is the single most important step, and the one people skip. Draft — generate an appropriate response, often with an AI step guided by a tight prompt and the context you gathered. Act — send the reply, or route it to a human for approval, and log the outcome back to the CRM so nothing falls through the cracks. Every reliable email automation is a variation on this: trigger, gather context, classify, draft, then act — with logging throughout. Tap the diagram to open it full-screen. Classify before you generate The temptation with AI is to skip straight to "let the model write a reply to anything." That's how you end up sending a cheerful sales pitch to someone who wrote "please remove me from your list." The fix is to classify intent first , then let each category follow its own path. A reply that clearly says "not interested" should trigger a polite unsubscribe and a CRM update — not an AI-written persuas

pages.t: Character Over Career: Five Choices
pages.h: Character over career: five choices I live by
pages.d: Character over career, satisfaction over success, failure over fear, people over place, goal over gossip — five choices that guide how I live and work.
pages.b: Character Over Career: Five Choices Mindset Character over career: five choices I live by Here is a small habit that runs my life. For a handful of words that start with the same letter, there are two things you could chase. Most people chase one of them. I've learned to chase the other. Same letter, different choice — and the choice makes all the difference. Published 27 July 2026 · 6 min read · by Krunalkumar Shah None of these are original virtues — you've heard all ten words before. What I find useful is the pairing: putting the two side by side forces an actual choice, and the choice reveals what you really value when both options are on the table. Here are the five I keep coming back to. The word on the left is the one I try to choose when both are within reach. Tap the diagram to open it full-screen. Character over Career Too many people quietly trade away their moral responsibilities for a paycheck and a better title — the duty they owe their parents, their family, the people who depend on them — because a career seems to demand it. I think that trade is backwards. Character isn't the thing you sacrifice for a career; it's the thing that opens career doors in the first place. Build a reputation for being dependable, honest, and decent, and opportunities come looking for you. A career is what you have; character is who you are while you build it. Careers can be rebuilt after a setback — I've watched people recover from layoffs, failed startups, and false starts. But a reputation for how you treat people, once broken, almost never comes back. I would rather be known as someone you can trust than someone you're impressed by. The impressive fades; the trustworthy compounds. When the two ever pull in different directions, character wins, because it's the only one of the two you actually keep. Satisfaction over Success Success is measured from the outside, and the goalposts never stop moving — there is always a bigger title, a higher number, someone one rung above you. Satisfaction is measured from the inside: did the work mean something, did it help someone, would I do it again. My first paid mentoring session earned me six dollars an hour. By any definition of success, that is nothing. By the measure of satisfaction, it was everything — it told me this work was worth doing, and it pointed my whole path. Chase success and you may never feel like you've arrived. Chase satisfaction and you can be at peace on the way up. Failure over Fear Given the choice

pages.t: Digital Arrest, Explained
pages.h: "Digital arrest": the scam that keeps you on camera until the money moves
pages.d: There is no such thing as a digital arrest. How the fake-police video-call scam works, why it fools careful people, and what to do in the first hour.
pages.b: Digital Arrest, Explained Security "Digital arrest": the scam that keeps you on camera until the money moves A caller in uniform tells you a parcel in your name held contraband, or that your Aadhaar turned up in a money-laundering case. Then comes the sentence the whole fraud rests on: stay on this video call, and tell nobody. This is how that call is built, why it works on people who are not fools, and exactly what to do — including the conversation to have with your parents before it ever rings. Published 31 August 2026 · 20 min read · by Krunalkumar Shah There is no such thing as a digital arrest If you read nothing else here, read this. "Digital arrest" is not a legal term, not a procedure, and not a power any Indian agency holds. It does not appear in the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, the Information Technology Act, or any rule made under them. No police force, no CBI officer, no Narcotics Control Bureau team, no Enforcement Directorate official, no customs officer and certainly nobody from TRAI has ever placed a person under arrest over a video call, because the law does not contain a way to do it. An arrest in India is a physical act performed by a person who is standing in front of you. The arrested person must be told the grounds of arrest, is entitled to consult a lawyer, and must be produced before a magistrate within twenty-four hours — a guarantee that sits in Article 22 of the Constitution and is repeated in the BNSS. Custody means a place, with a register, and a magistrate at the end of the day. None of that survives translation to a WhatsApp video call, which is why no version of it exists. There is no lawful arrest that happens on a screen, no lawful custody you serve in your own bedroom, and no lawful account you pay into to clear your name. Three more absolutes worth memorizing, because every variant of the scam breaks at least one of them. No Indian investigating agency will ask you to stay on camera. No Indian agency operates a "verification account", an "RBI escrow account", or a "refundable security deposit" that clears your name. No genuine investigation requires you to keep it secret from your family. Those three sentences are enough to defeat the entire fraud, and they hold no matter how convincing the uniform, the case number, or the document is. pages.t: Finding the Right Career
pages.h: Finding the right career when everyone has an opinion
pages.d: Follow your passion is bad advice. Here is a more honest method: three things that must overlap, testing instead of deciding, and what to ignore.
pages.b: Finding the Right Career Career & Mentorship Finding the right career when everyone has an opinion I have sat in more than five thousand technical interviews and mentored a lot of people through the first decade of their working life. The single most common thing I hear is not "I cannot get a job." It is "I do not know if this is the right thing to be doing at all." That question deserves a better answer than the one people usually get. Published 27 August 2026 · 8 min read · by Krunalkumar Shah Why "follow your passion" fails so many people It assumes the passion already exists, fully formed, waiting to be discovered. For a small number of people that is true. For most it is not, and being told otherwise produces a specific kind of misery: the belief that everyone else received a calling and you were skipped. What actually happens for most people is the reverse. Interest follows competence. You get moderately good at something, the work stops being frustrating, you start seeing the interesting problems inside it that were invisible from outside — and somewhere in there it becomes a thing you care about. Passion is far more often a result of getting good at something than the reason you started. If you are waiting to feel certain before you commit, you have the order backwards. Commitment for long enough to become competent is usually what produces the certainty. Three things that have to overlap A career that holds up over decades tends to sit where three things meet. Miss any one and you can predict the failure mode. Something you can become genuinely good at. Not something you are good at today — aptitude at eighteen tells you very little. Something where you improve at a reasonable rate and the improvement is visible to you. Something someone will pay for. This is not a compromise of your ideals, it is the difference between a career and a hobby. Both are worth having. Only one pays rent. Something you can sustain. Not "love every day" — nobody loves every day. Can you do this on an ordinary Tuesday when it is boring, without it costing you your health or the people you care about? Miss one and here is what you get: Good at it and paid, but cannot sustain it — the classic burnout track. Often lucrative right up until it is not. Good at it and sustainable, but nobody pays — a wonderful hobby. Keep it as one. Paid and sustainable, but you never get good — the quiet one. pages.t: The First Week of an Automation Job
pages.h: What actually happens in the first week of an automation engagement
pages.d: Week one of an automation engagement buys a map and a decision, not a running bot. What gets read, what gets counted, and what should not be automated.
pages.b: The First Week of an Automation Job Automation What actually happens in the first week of an automation engagement If you are paying someone to automate a process, the first week is not building. It is reading the process as it actually runs, counting it, and deciding which parts deserve a machine — including the parts that deserve deleting instead. Here is that week in the order it happens, and what goes wrong in it. Published 31 August 2026 · 9 min read · by Krunalkumar Shah What week one actually produces If you hire someone to automate a process, the reasonable expectation is that by Friday something is running. That is not what my first week produces, and I would rather say so before you pay for it than after. Week one produces two things. The first is a map: a written description of the process as it actually runs, with the systems named, the people named, the volume counted and the failure points marked. The second is a decision — which parts to automate, which to fix by hand first, and which to delete. An automation is a machine that repeats a decision. If the decision is wrong, or the process is about to change, or the whole thing runs four times a month, nobody has saved anything: you have bought a maintenance liability with a dashboard on it. The shape of the week, roughly, and it is rarely this tidy: Roughly when What happens What it produces Day 1 Discovery conversation; access requested in writing Named systems, named people, open questions Days 1–3 Waiting on read-only access, and chasing it Usually the longest queue of the week Day 2 or 3 Watching one real run, start to finish The process as run, not as described Days 3–4 Counting volume, duration and error rate from exports Baseline numbers with sources attached Day 5 Writing the map, the exclusions and the quote A document, and a decision that is yours The limit of that argument: for small work a week is overkill. One trigger, one system, one person, low consequence if it breaks — then a call and one observed run is the whole of discovery, and I say so rather than selling five days. The threshold I use is soft: more than two systems, or more than two people, and discovery earns its cost. I have not measured that boundary. Day one: the conversation, and the questions that matter Day one is a conversation, usually an hour or two, with whoever owns the outcome and — if I can get them — whoever actually does the work. pages.t: Git, Explained From the Object Up
pages.h: Git, explained from the object up
pages.d: Git stops being spells once you know what it stores. The object model, the three trees, what each command actually moves, and the undo toolbox — deeply.
pages.b: Git, Explained From the Object Up Engineering practice Git, explained from the object up Most people use git the way people once used incantations: type this, hope, type it harder. It works until the first merge conflict, the first detached HEAD, the first force-push panic. The cure is not memorising more commands. It is knowing the three things any command can move — because once you can see what git actually stores, every command becomes obvious, including the frightening ones. This week I rewrote 169 commits on this site without changing a byte of content; that is only a sane thing to do if you know exactly what is underneath. Here is what is underneath. Published 29 August 2026 · 12 min read · by Krunalkumar Shah The three things git can move Every git command you will ever run manipulates some combination of exactly three places, and the documentation rarely says so out loud. The working tree is the folder you can see — ordinary files, the ones your editor touches. The index (the docs also say "staging area") is git's private draft of your next commit. And the history is a graph of commits, with a handful of named labels pointing into it, one of which — HEAD — marks where you are standing. That is the whole machine. git add copies a file from the working tree into the index. git commit turns the index into a permanent snapshot and moves your branch label forward. git diff compares two of the three places. The commands that frighten people — reset , checkout , rebase — are frightening only because they move more than one of the three at once, silently. Learn the three places and you stop memorising commands; you start predicting them. What a commit actually is Git does not store diffs. It stores snapshots , whole ones, in a content-addressed object store — a small database living in the .git folder. A file's content is stored as a blob . A folder is a tree : a list of names pointing at blobs and other trees. A commit is a tiny text record that points at one tree — the complete state of your project at that moment — plus its parent commit or commits, an author, a date, and a message. Every one of these objects is named by a hash of its own content (SHA-1 in almost every repository you will meet). Change one character of a message and the hash changes, which means the "name" of a commit is its content. Nothing in the store can be edited in place, ever. Git only writes new objects. pages.t: How Cybercrime Cases Are Solved
pages.h: How cybercrime cases are solved: from first alert to the courtroom
pages.d: From first alert to the courtroom: incident response, police investigation, digital forensics, and what makes electronic evidence stand in court.
pages.b: How Cybercrime Cases Are Solved Security How cybercrime cases are solved: from first alert to the courtroom A breach or an online fraud starts two clocks at once — the victim's race to contain the damage, and the investigator's race to preserve the evidence. This is the full lifecycle of a cybercrime case: the incident-response track, the law-enforcement track, the digital forensics where they meet, and the courtroom where it all gets tested. Published 10 August 2026 · 14 min read · by Krunalkumar Shah Two clocks start when something breaks The moment a ransomware note appears on a screen, or money leaves an account it shouldn't have, two clocks start ticking. The first is the containment clock : stop the bleeding, get systems back, keep the business alive. The second is the evidence clock : everything you will ever be able to prove about what happened is decaying — logs are rotating, RAM is volatile, and stolen money is hopping between mule accounts. These clocks pull in opposite directions, and most of the damage to a cybercrime case — as opposed to the damage from the crime itself — happens in the first few hours, before any forensic examiner or investigating officer arrives. Not through malice; through reflex. The IT team wipes the infected laptop. The embarrassed victim deletes the chat. The company "handles it quietly" and calls the police three weeks later, when the trail is stone cold. By the time an expert shows up, the case has usually already been strengthened or crippled by people who never realized they were handling evidence. This article walks the whole lifecycle: the victim's track (incident response), the law-enforcement track (complaint to charge sheet), the digital forensics where the two converge, and the admissibility rules that decide what survives in court. The legal specifics are Indian — the portal, the helpline, the statutes — but the discipline underneath is the same everywhere. Track one: the victim side of the case Incident response has a standard shape, and the one most teams borrow is the NIST lifecycle (SP 800-61): preparation , detection and analysis , containment, eradication and recovery , and post-incident activity . Real incidents loop through these phases rather than marching through them. The phase where cases are won or lost is containment — that is where the two clocks collide head-on. pages.t: How I Vibe Coded This Website
pages.h: How I vibe coded this website — and the mechanism that made it hold
pages.d: I described what I wanted, an AI built it, and I kept the authority. The specification, review and gates that turned vibe coding into engineering.
pages.b: How I Vibe Coded This Website Engineering practice How I vibe coded this website — and the mechanism that made it hold I did not hand-write most of this site. I described what I wanted, an AI produced it, and I kept the authority over every decision that mattered. That is the easy half to explain and the wrong half to copy. What actually made it survive is the mechanism I built around the prompting — how I specify, how I verify, and what happens when something breaks. This is that mechanism, with the receipts. Published 21 August 2026 · 11 min read · by Krunalkumar Shah What vibe coding actually got me Let me be honest about the starting point, because the honesty is the useful part. I described pages in plain English and a model wrote them. The first version of this site existed in an afternoon. If you have tried it, you know the feeling — it is genuinely fast, and the output is genuinely fine. It is fine for about a week. The trouble is not that the code is bad. The trouble is that you did not build a system, you accumulated one. Nothing records why the header is structured the way it is. Nothing stops the next change from quietly contradicting the last one. You cannot answer "is this still correct?" because you never wrote down what correct meant. Ask for one more feature and you get one more layer on a foundation nobody documented, including you. This site is 186 pages now — 62 of them browser-based labs that run real language runtimes, 67 games, 27 blog posts, the rest ordinary pages — across more than 160 commits, with zero npm dependencies. Nothing that size survives on vibes. What follows is the scaffolding that let it get there while I was still the one deciding. The prompt is a specification The single biggest change in my output quality had nothing to do with the model. It was realising that a prompt is not a wish. It is a specification, and it should be written like one. "Make the blog look nicer" is a wish. It produces something, you squint at it, you ask again. Three rounds later you have drifted somewhere nobody chose. Compare that with what a real request looks like — the constraints first, the ask second: What a usable spec contains. The goal in one sentence. The constraints that must hold no matter what. The things that must not change. How I will know it worked. And the cases I already know are hard. pages.t: How a SIM Swap Works
pages.h: How a SIM swap works, and why an OTP is not the protection you think it is
pages.d: How a SIM swap actually happens: the two ways a number changes hands, why SMS was never an authentication channel, and the defences that hold.
pages.b: How a SIM Swap Works Security How a SIM swap works, and why an OTP is not the protection you think it is A SIM swap breaks no encryption and exploits no software. It moves one record at a telecom operator so that your number answers on somebody else's SIM, and then collects everything the rest of the world sends to that number in the belief that it is talking to you. The interesting part is not the theft. It is that a control most Indian banks still treat as proof of identity comes down, in the end, to a person at a counter deciding whether the customer in front of them is who they say they are. Published 31 August 2026 · 21 min read · by Krunalkumar Shah What a SIM swap actually is Your SIM holds a secret key that proves to the network which subscription it belongs to. In a SIM swap, that key is not extracted, copied or broken. What changes is a record on the operator's side: the association between your number and a SIM profile is repointed at a different card. A replacement SIM issued at a retail point, or a port of the number to a different operator altogether, both end in the same state — the network now delivers calls and messages for your number somewhere else, and the card sitting in your phone belongs to a subscription that no longer exists. Nothing in that description is a flaw. Operators must be able to reissue a number, because people lose phones, break SIM trays, drop handsets in water, and change networks. The capability is necessary. The attack is not on the capability but on the procedure that decides whether the person requesting it is the subscriber, and that procedure is, at its last step, a human judgement. It is worth separating this from SIM cloning , which is what a lot of coverage calls it. Cloning means copying the card's secret key onto a second card so that two SIMs answer to one identity. That was practical against early SIM generations and is genuinely hard against the ones deployed today. It is also almost never what has happened when somebody's accounts empty overnight. The common event is the boring one: a form, a counter, and an approval. There is no cryptography in this attack. There is an identity check performed by a person who has a queue behind them, a target to hit, and a checklist of details that the person in front of them can recite. pages.t: How to brief a security consultant
pages.h: How to brief a security consultant so the quote is accurate
pages.d: A vague brief buys a wide quote, and the width is the consultant pricing their uncertainty. Here is what to supply so the number means something.
pages.b: How to brief a security consultant Security How to brief a security consultant so the quote is accurate A vague brief does not get you a cheap quote. It gets you a wide one, because the consultant is pricing the range of things your system might turn out to be — and you pay for that range either way. This is what to put in the brief, and why each item moves the number. Published 31 August 2026 · 9 min read · by Krunalkumar Shah The width of the quote is the guess Send the same one-line request to three security firms — “we need a security test of our platform” — and the numbers that come back are usually hard to compare. The instinct is to read the spread as one firm being greedy and another being cheap. Sometimes that is exactly what it is. More often all three read the same vague sentence, made different assumptions about what sits behind it, and priced their own assumptions. Here is the part that is easy to miss as a buyer. When a consultant cannot see the size of the work, they do not price the work. They price the work plus the range of things it might turn out to be. That padding is not dishonest — it is the only rational response to a request for a fixed number covering an unknown quantity. You pay for it either way: if the job turns out small you overpaid, and if it turns out large you get a change request anyway, because the padding was a guess too. A vague brief does not buy you a cheap quote. It buys you an expensive one with the risk priced in, or a cheap one from somebody who has not understood the job yet. So the width of a quote is information: it says the consultant cannot see the edges of your system. The useful response is not to negotiate the number down but to remove the uncertainty that produced it. That costs nothing, and you are the only person who can do it. Four things you might be buying Before any technical detail, answer one question in a sentence: what has to be true when this is over? There are four common answers, and they are four different engagements. The word “pentest” gets used for all of them, which is how a buyer ends up paying adversarial-test rates for a list of patches, or handing a list of patches to a customer who wanted a signed report. pages.t: How to Read a Job Description
pages.h: How to read a job description
pages.d: How to read a job posting honestly: which requirements are load-bearing, what fast-paced and wear many hats really mean, and what a missing salary tells you.
pages.b: How to Read a Job Description Career & Mentorship How to read a job description A posting looks like a document with an author, and it almost never has one. Some of what is in there is a real requirement, some is a wish somebody added in a meeting, and some is a warning about the job that nobody meant to publish. Reading it literally is the most common expensive mistake I see in the people I mentor. This is how to read one instead. Published 31 August 2026 · 23 min read · by Krunalkumar Shah Who actually writes a posting Start with the production process, because everything else follows from it. A job posting is assembled rather than written. The hiring manager describes roughly what is needed. A recruiter reshapes it into the format the careers page expects and adds the keywords the applicant tracking system will search on. Somebody in HR pastes in the standard paragraphs. Two people who will work with the hire add a line each, usually about the thing that hurt them last quarter. A senior person adds something aspirational. And whoever is short of time copies half of the last posting for a different role, because that file is the one already open. The result is a union of everybody's preferences rather than an intersection of what the job requires. Nobody in that chain is being dishonest. It is just that no single person owns the total, and nobody is accountable for the list being shorter than it needs to be. A second force keeps it inflated. Everyone on the writing side knows the list is negotiable, so adding a line costs nothing and removing one feels like giving something away. Asking for more than you need is free; asking for exactly what you need risks getting less. When both sides understand that convention, the inflation is harmless. The person it hurts is the reader who does not know the convention exists — and that reader is disproportionately the one applying for their first or second job. A third force is mechanical. Some requirements are there to be filterable rather than because anybody believes them. "Bachelor's degree in Computer Science or a related field" is very often a checkbox with a filter behind it, not a considered position on degrees. So is a years-of-experience number that ends in a zero or a five. There is an important exception, and it is worth learning to spot because it inverts all the advice below. Published 31 August 2026 · 10 min read · by Krunalkumar Shah Search it, do not read it A privacy policy is a reference document laid out like an essay. Read it from the top and you spend your attention on definitions and reassurance, and reach the paragraph that matters several minutes in, by which point you have stopped caring. That is not bad writing; it is what a document looks like when it must satisfy a regulator, a lawyer and a marketing team at once. So do not read it. Search it. Open the page, press Ctrl+F — Cmd+F on a Mac — and run these terms in roughly this order. Each lands in the paragraph that answers one question. third part — truncated on purpose, so one search catches “third party”, “third parties” and “third-party”. share and sell — two different verbs for where your data goes. They sit in different paragraphs and do not mean the same thing. affiliate — a company in the same corporate group. Sharing inside the group is often carved out of promises made elsewhere. retain — how long they keep it. delete — how you get out. legal basis — says at once whether this is a GDPR-shaped policy. transfer — catches cross-border transfers and the acquisition clause, the one nearly everybody misses. children — the age line, and a fair proxy for how carefully the document was written. change — how the policy itself can change underneath you. Nine searches. A search that returns nothing is a finding too: a policy with no occurrence of “retain” has not told you how long it keeps your data. Read sharing first, because that is the business model Of the nine, sharing is the one to read properly and to read first. Most of a privacy policy is housekeeping: what a cookie is, that they use encryption, that they care about you. The sharing section is the business. If a company makes money from data rather than from you, this is where it has to say so. Two different things hide under the same word. pages.b: Standing Out in an Internship Interview Careers How to stand out in an internship interview Between 2021 and 2023, while working at MountBlue and consulting for US firms, I took more than 5,000 interviews. That much time on the other side of the table teaches you what actually separates candidates — and it's rarely what they spent their time preparing. Here's what actually moves the needle, from someone who has done the reviewing at scale. Published 24 June 2026 · 6 min read · by Krunalkumar Shah Understand what an internship interview is really for A senior-hire interview asks "can you already do this job?" An internship interview asks a very different question: "will you be worth teaching?" Nobody expects an intern to know everything. What they are actually screening for is coachability, curiosity, and whether you finish what you start. Once you understand that shift, half of interview anxiety disappears — you stop trying to fake expertise you aren't expected to have, and start showing the traits that actually get you picked. Attitude first, aptitude second If those 5,000-plus interviews taught me one thing, it's this: I screen for attitude before aptitude. It sounds backwards — surely skill is what matters? — but the logic is simple. Aptitude can be added. I can teach a framework, a language, a tool; skills are learnable on a timeline. Attitude comes from within, and no amount of training installs it. Curiosity, honesty, the willingness to keep going when something is hard, the instinct to take ownership instead of making excuses — you either bring those to the table or you don't. So a candidate who is a little behind on skills but clearly hungry, coachable, and honest will beat a more polished one who is arrogant or passive nearly every time. What this means for you is freeing: you do not have to walk in as the finished article. You have to walk in as someone obviously worth investing in. Show the attitude, and the aptitude gap stops being disqualifying — it becomes the exact thing the internship exists to close. Do the homework almost nobody does You would be surprised how many candidates can't answer "so, what do you know about my work?" Turning up informed is rare enough that it instantly separates you. Before any interview: Read what the person or company actually does — their projects, their writing, their focus areas — and be able to name one specific thing that interested you and why . pages.b: How to Succeed in Software Development Craft How to succeed in software development: the four-step path After years of building systems and reviewing thousands of engineers, I've come to trust one simple order of operations. Great software isn't written in one heroic pass — it's grown through four stages: make it work, make it modular, make it readable, then make it optimized. The magic is entirely in doing them in that order. Published 5 June 2026 · 5 min read · by Krunalkumar Shah Why the order matters more than the steps Most people fail at software not because they can't do these four things, but because they do them in the wrong sequence. They optimize before it works. They polish readability on code they're about to throw away. They chase a perfectly modular architecture for a problem they don't understand yet. Each of those is effort spent in the wrong place at the wrong time. The four steps below are valuable precisely because they tell you what to care about now and what to deliberately ignore until later. Each step stands on the one before it. Skip a stair and the ones above it wobble. Tap the diagram to open it full-screen. Step 1 — Make it work The first and only job at the start is to get something running end to end, however ugly. One long function, hard-coded values, no error handling worth mentioning — fine. The goal here is not quality; it is proof . A working-but-messy version teaches you what the problem actually is, surfaces the surprises hiding in the requirements, and gives you something real to improve. A beautiful design for the wrong problem is worthless, and you can't know the right problem until something works. The trap at this stage is perfectionism — polishing code you might delete once you understand the problem better. Resist it. Get to working first, and give yourself explicit permission for it to be rough. Step 2 — Make it modular Now that it works, you understand the problem well enough to see its natural seams. Modularity is the step where you break that one big blob into pieces that each do a single job — a function that only parses, a function that only validates, a function that only sends. Good modules have clear boundaries: you can understand one without holding all the others in your head, and you can change one without breaking its neighbors. The trouble starts when someone actually answers. Replies arrive at all hours, in every shape — "interested, send more info", "book me a call", "not interested", out-of-office bounces, and the occasional message that defies categorization. An SDR now has to read each one, figure out what it is, write a response in the company's voice, and follow up if the prospect goes quiet. Response speed matters enormously here, and it's precisely when the team is busiest that replies sit unanswered the longest. That grind is what CleverResponder removes. Not by letting an AI run wild in the inbox — by giving the boring 80% of replies a fast, safe, supervised path, so humans only touch the messages that need them. What it does, end to end Receives every campaign reply through a webhook, the moment it lands. Classifies it — interested, info requested, meeting requested, not interested, out of office, and more. Drafts a reply with AI, grounded in a knowledge document of FAQs and company details — so answers come from your facts, not the model's imagination. Sends and follows up — approved replies go out; meeting requests get a calendar link, and if no booking happens within a few days, the workflow checks in and nudges. pages.b: India's IT Law, Explained: IT Act to DPDP Security India's IT law, explained: from the IT Act 2000 to the DPDP era India's digital economy runs on a legal stack most practitioners have never actually read — an e-commerce law from 2000, criminal teeth bolted on in 2008, a thickening rules layer, and now a full data-protection regime. Here is the whole structure in one pass: what each layer says, the folklore worth unlearning, and a reference index you can bookmark. Published 10 August 2026 · Updated 17 August 2026 · 16 min read · by Krunalkumar Shah The law stack nobody reads If you build or run anything digital in India, you are already inside this stack: every UPI payment, SaaS security clause, and police complaint quoting Section 66C traces back to a handful of statutes and their rules. Yet most of us meet the law only in fragments, and fragments breed folklore — misquoted sections, invented penalties, a provision struck down a decade ago still cited in complaints. I am not a lawyer — I am a security practitioner who kept meeting these laws in audits, vendor contracts, and incident calls until I read the primary texts. This is the orientation I wish someone had handed me — every claim checked against its primary source and date-stamped where the ground is moving. Not legal advice. This is practitioner orientation — a map of the terrain, not counsel about your situation. For a notice, a summons, an investigation, or a compliance decision, consult a lawyer qualified in Indian law. Verified against primary sources in August 2026; where the law is in flux, I say so. Twenty-five years of Indian IT law in one line — the timeline this article walks. Tap the diagram to open it full-screen. The IT Act 2000: why it exists In the late 1990s India had a practical problem: contract and evidence law assumed paper. A "document" was something you could hold; a "signature" meant ink. So when the United Nations adopted the UNCITRAL Model Law on Electronic Commerce (1996) and recommended that member states legislate along its lines, India did. The Information Technology Act, 2000 came into force on 17 October 2000 — the country's first comprehensive law for electronic commerce and computer crime. Its founding achievements sound mundane precisely because they worked: electronic records and digital signatures gained legal validity , so a contract no longer fails merely for being electronic; the Controller of Certifying Authorities (CCA) was created to license the authorities

A single $6 session started more than I realized at the time. Published 19 July 2026 · 9 min read · by Krunalkumar Shah The classroom that didn't feel like enough I earned my bachelor's in engineering from a private state college, then a master's focused on information security. On paper that is a clean line. In reality, the classroom always felt like it was describing the world rather than letting me touch it. Lectures could tell me how a system was supposed to behave; they couldn't show me how it broke when someone poked it the wrong way. That gap — between knowing about something and having actually done it — is the thing that has shaped every decision since. So I started building and breaking things on my own machine. Most of it went nowhere. But one of those late-night rabbit holes turned into the first real milestone of my career. The paper I almost didn't write I got curious about a deceptively simple attack: the fork bomb. A tiny snippet that tells a system to endlessly copy itself until it grinds to a halt. What fascinated me was that even a properly hardened Linux machine could be brought down by it, because creating a process is a completely ordinary thing that needs no special permission. The existing defenses all had a catch — they either blocked legitimate work or punished innocent programs forever. I thought I had an idea for something better, and I nearly talked myself out of writing it up. Who was I to publish? A student. But I did the work, ran the experiments, and it became a peer-reviewed paper — Security Against Fork Bomb Attack in Linux Based Systems , published in IJRAT. It earned a silver medal from Shantilal Shah Government Engineering College and IPCL, and was nominated for a best-paper award by the International Association of Engineers (IAENG). The lesson wasn't "I'm brilliant." It was that the gap between an idea and a published result is mostly just the willingness to actually finish. pages.b: n8n vs Make vs Zapier, Compared Automation n8n, Make, or Zapier: an honest comparison I build automation for a living — HubSpot, n8n, Make and Zapier, in production, for clients who notice when it breaks. Most comparisons of these three are feature tables, and feature tables do not decide anything any more. The thing that decides it is where the workflow runs and who is liable when it goes wrong. Everything else is downstream of that. Published 31 August 2026 · 23 min read · by Krunalkumar Shah The decision that actually matters Open any of the three and you will find the same building blocks. A trigger. A branch. A step that calls an HTTP endpoint. A step where you can write JavaScript because the visual thing ran out of road. A library of prebuilt connectors for whatever software the client actually uses. The gaps between them are real but they are narrow, and they close a little every quarter, which is why a feature table written today is a stale document by the time somebody reads it. Here is the column the feature tables do not have: When this workflow runs at three in the morning, whose computer is it running on, and whose name is on the incident report if that computer is breached? Zapier and Make are hosted products. There is no self-hosted edition, by design — the uptime and the connector maintenance are what you are buying. That means your client's records pass through a third party's infrastructure on every run, the run history sitting in that infrastructure contains the actual field values rather than a summary of them, and the OAuth tokens for every system you connected are stored there too. If your contract enumerates subprocessors, they go on the list. n8n can be self-hosted. A container, a Postgres database, a machine you rent. Nothing about the workflow touches an intermediary at all. That is the entire argument, and it is the only argument that survives a conversation with a legal team. Let me be fair before this reads as a pitch for self-hosting. That constraint applies to roughly one project in four. If nobody has mentioned data residency, nobody has a data processing agreement, and the payload is marketing emails, then a hosted vendor's security posture is almost certainly better than the one I would put together on a virtual server for a small client. Choosing self-hosted n8n for a five-step Zap-shaped job is not rigour. It is an unnecessary server for someone to forget about. But get the order right. Answer the hosting question first

pages.b: Passwords and Passkeys: What Protects You Security Passwords, passkeys, and what actually protects you Almost nobody loses an account because somebody guessed their password. They lose it because the same password was used somewhere that got breached, or because they typed it into a page that looked right and was not. Understanding which threat is which is the difference between security advice that helps and security advice that just makes your life harder. Published 27 August 2026 · 9 min read · by Krunalkumar Shah How accounts are actually lost There are four common routes, and they are not equally likely. Ranked roughly by how often they land: Reuse after somebody else's breach. A site you signed up to years ago is compromised, and the email-and-password pair from it gets replayed against your bank, your mail, your everything. This is credential stuffing , and it requires no cracking at all — the password is already correct. You can check whether a password of yours appears in known breach data using the breach checker , which does it by k-anonymity so the password never leaves your browser. Phishing. You are sent somewhere convincing and you type the password in yourself. No technical weakness in your password is involved. A long random one is phished exactly as easily as a short one. Pull a suspicious link apart before you visit it and you will see how much a URL can hide. Offline cracking after a breach. If the breached site stored passwords badly, attackers grind through them. How long that takes depends almost entirely on the site's choices, not yours — billions of guesses per second against MD5 , a few thousand against bcrypt . You can watch that difference happen in the hash cracker . Actual online guessing. Rare, because every serious service rate-limits it. This is the threat most password advice is written for, and it is the one that matters least. Three of those four are unaffected by how clever your password is. That is the whole reason the industry is moving on. What still matters about passwords Two things, and only two. Length, not decoration. Substituting 3 for e adds essentially nothing — cracking tools have known that trick for decades. Adding words adds real entropy . Four unrelated words beat P@ssw0rd! by an enormous margin and are far easier to type. Measure it rather than guess : the difference is not subtle. Never reusing them. pages.b: How to Read a Data Breach Notification Security How to read a data breach notification "We recently became aware of an incident." Every word after that opening was chosen, reviewed by a lawyer, and written to be true on the worst set of facts the company could not rule out. That is not dishonesty — it is what careful drafting under legal exposure produces. But it means the email is a document to be read rather than a message to be believed, and the reading is a skill. Here is the vocabulary, the dates that are missing, and what to actually do — which depends almost entirely on which fields leaked. Published 31 August 2026 · 26 min read · by Krunalkumar Shah The email is a legal document A breach notification is written by a small committee. Security supplies the facts that are established, which is usually fewer than everyone expects. Legal decides which of those facts must be stated, which may be stated, and which sentence structures survive being read out in a proceeding two years later. Communications makes it readable. Nobody in that room is trying to mislead you, and nearly everybody in that room is trying to avoid asserting something that later turns out to be wrong. The result is a particular register. Claims about the company's own actions are definite: we contained, we engaged, we notified. Claims about what happened to your data are hedged: may have been, potentially, could have included. Claims about consequences are negative: we have no evidence of. Once you notice that the confidence in each sentence is set by who is in a position to know, the document starts telling you a great deal — not by what it says, but by which parts it refuses to say plainly. So the reading technique is simple and slightly adversarial. For each sentence, ask two questions. What would have to be true for this sentence to be true? And what would the sentence have said if the facts were better? A company that could write "no data left our systems" writes that, because it is excellent news. A company that writes "we have no evidence that data was removed" is telling you it could not establish the good version. You are not looking for lies. You are looking for the shape of what the writer could not say. The hedge is the finding. The vocabulary, decoded Five phrases do most of the work in most notifications. pages.h: Scope the work before you quote it
pages.d: Most bad projects are not underpriced, they are under-scoped. Five questions to answer before you send a number, and how to change scope without resentment.
pages.b: Scope the Work Before You Quote It Business Scope the work before you quote it Nearly every project I have watched go wrong went wrong in the same place, and it was not the price. It was the sentence that said what the work was — because there wasn't one. Scope is not paperwork you do after winning the job. It is the thing you are actually selling, and writing it down is the cheapest insurance either side will ever buy. Published 27 August 2026 · 7 min read · by Krunalkumar Shah Under-priced and under-defined are not the same problem When a project loses money, the reflex is to conclude you charged too little. Sometimes that is true. Far more often the rate was fine and the boundary was missing — so the work kept growing while the number stayed still. Doubling your rate does not fix that. It just means you lose more slowly on a job that has no edges. You can tell the two apart with one question: if the work had stopped where you both originally imagined, would the price have been fair? If yes, you did not have a pricing problem. You had a definition problem. A scope is not a list of tasks. It is a description of the edge — what is inside, what is outside, and what has to be true for the inside to be possible. The five questions to answer before you send a number None of these are clever. They are simply the five things that, when left unanswered, later turn into an argument. Answer them in writing, in the client's own words where you can, and most of the argument never happens. 1. What does "done" look like, observably? Not "improve the onboarding flow" — that has no end. "A new user can sign up, verify their email, and reach the dashboard without support contact." That has an end, and both of you can see it from across the room. 2. What is explicitly not included? This is the sentence people skip because it feels negative, and it is the single highest-value line in the document. If you are hardening a web application, say plainly that it does not cover the mail server, the staff laptops, or the third-party plugin they bought last year. 3. What do you need from them, and by when? Access, credentials, a decision-maker, sample data, a staging environment. Most delays that get blamed on the contractor were actually a week spent waiting for a login. Name the dependency and name the date. 4. How many rounds of revision? Sort the seven that way — with the requirements that matter in practice — and it becomes obvious which are obligations, which are choices, and which are actually yours. Published 10 August 2026 · 12 min read · by Krunalkumar Shah Compliance is trust made auditable Every security consulting conversation I have eventually lands on the same question. Not "how do we stop attackers" — that one comes with the territory — but some version of: "GDPR, HIPAA, SOC 2, ISO-something… which of these actually apply to us?" It comes from founders, engineering leads, and operations people holding a 300-question vendor questionnaire — always in the same slightly exhausted tone. It's a fair question, because the alphabet soup hides a real distinction: these frameworks are not the same kind of thing. Some are laws, with regulators and fines behind them. One is a contract you accepted the day you started taking card payments. Some are voluntary standards you can certify against, and one is an accountant's opinion about you. Mix those categories up and you get the classic failure mode I keep meeting: a company proudly chasing a certificate it doesn't need while ignoring a law that already applies to it. Here is the framing that unlocks all of it: compliance is trust made auditable. Every framework below turns "trust us with your data" into something a third party can verify. And every one of them is a floor, not a ceiling — the minimum a regulator, bank, or customer will accept, not a level attackers find inconvenient. The attack families I mapped in the previous post do not check your certification status before firing. The lay of the land: seven frameworks in one table Before the deep dives, orientation. The most useful column is the second one — what kind of thing is this? — because it tells you who enforces the framework and what actually happens when you fall short. pages.t: Smart Feedback: How to Give and Receive
pages.h: Smart feedback: how to give and receive it
pages.d: Why vague praise fails, a three-part structure for feedback that actually helps, and how to receive criticism without getting defensive.
pages.b: Smart Feedback: How to Give and Receive Mentorship Smart feedback: how to give and receive it Feedback is the engine of growth, and most of it is wasted — too vague to act on, too harsh to hear, or too polite to matter. After years of mentoring, here is how I try to give feedback that actually helps, and how to take it without your defenses swallowing the lesson. Published 15 June 2026 · 4 min read · by Krunalkumar Shah Why most feedback does nothing "Good job." "This could be better." "I didn't love it." These feel like feedback, but they change nothing, because the person receiving them has no idea what to actually do differently. Vague praise is pleasant and useless. Vague criticism is unpleasant and useless. Both fail for the same reason: they describe a feeling instead of pointing at a specific, changeable thing. Useful feedback is specific, actionable, and kind — and the order matters. Specific so the person knows exactly what you mean. Actionable so they know what to do next. Kind so they can actually hear it instead of bracing against it. Miss any one of those and the feedback simply gets ignored, no matter how right you were. A simple structure I keep coming back to When I give feedback, I try to hit three beats in order. It stops me from being vague and keeps the conversation forward-looking: Observation — the specific thing I noticed, stated as a fact, not a judgment. pages.b: Surface, Deep, and Dark Web, Explained Security Surface web, deep web, and dark web: what the three layers actually are Almost every explanation of this starts with an iceberg, and the iceberg is wrong in the way that matters most. These are not three depths of one ocean. They are three different answers to a single question: who can reach this page, and how? Get that straight and the rest — including the part that gets sold to you as fear — stops being mysterious. Published 31 August 2026 · 15 min read · by Krunalkumar Shah The iceberg is the wrong picture You know the diagram. A small tip above the waterline labelled "4% — Google, Facebook, Wikipedia," a vast blue mass below it labelled "deep web," and at the very bottom, in red, a small dark chamber labelled with a skull. It is a memorable image, and it teaches three false things at once. The first is the arithmetic. Nobody can count the deep web, because most of it is not made of pages at all — it is a database that produces a page when you ask it something. How many pages does an airline's fare search have? As many as there are journeys you could type in. The percentages in the iceberg trace back to a paper written in 2001, about a web that no longer exists, and they have been copied forward ever since without anyone recounting. The second is the vertical axis itself. Depth implies that you pass through the deep web on your way down to the dark web, and that the deep web is a rougher neighbourhood than the surface. Neither is true. Your email inbox is not adjacent to a criminal market, and no amount of scrolling gets you from one to the other. The third is the implication that all of this is somewhere else . It is not. Two of the three layers are the ordinary web you use every day, and the third runs on the same wires as the other two. Replace depth with reachability and everything falls into place. Surface: something can follow a link to it. Deep: it needs credentials or a query first. Dark: it needs different software to route to it at all. Three answers to one question — not three floors of a building. The same three words, drawn by reachability instead of depth. Nothing is stacked, because depth was never the axis. Every business has all four, whether the founder names them or not — and the moment any one of them cracks, the whole structure starts to lean. Across all of it, the same pattern holds: a company is a structure resting on four M's. Three of them are the resources; the fourth is what turns those resources into results. Manpower, money, and mind are the pillars. Management is the foundation and beam that keeps them working together instead of apart. Tap the diagram to open it full-screen. 1. Manpower — the people who do the work Nothing gets built without people, and a business is only ever as strong as the people inside it. This is the pillar I know best, because I've spent thousands of interviews trying to judge it. The lesson from all those conversations is the one I keep repeating: hire for attitude first, aptitude second. Skills can be taught; character, curiosity, and ownership have to be there already. But manpower isn't just hiring — it's keeping good people and getting the best from them. A team of brilliant individuals who don't trust each other will lose to an average team that does. Culture, motivation, and how people are treated aren't soft extras; they're the difference between a workforce that carries the business and one that quietly drags it. 2. Reverse a linked list in place. A definition question I could mark right or wrong in my head while the candidate was still talking. All three felt rigorous. None of them told me anything I could not have read off a CV. What they measured was exposure. Somebody who had already met the puzzle answered it in forty seconds, and somebody who had not sat there being watched. The forty-second answer was not evidence of thinking; it was evidence of having met the puzzle. I was, in effect, grading people on how many interviews they had already failed. pages.h: The life of the Buddha, without the mythology
pages.d: Who Siddhattha Gotama actually was, what the earliest texts say, where the familiar legend was added later, and what he taught in forty-five years of walking.
pages.b: The Life of the Buddha, Without the Mythology Life The life of the Buddha, without the mythology Almost everything most of us know about the Buddha arrived through a long chain of retellings, and a good deal of it was added centuries after he died. That does not make the story less interesting — it makes it more so, because underneath the gold leaf there is a person who lived, taught for forty-five years, and was unusually insistent that nobody take his word for anything. Published 27 August 2026 · 10 min read · by Krunalkumar Shah What we can actually say about him He was born Siddhattha Gotama — Siddhārtha Gautama in Sanskrit — into the Śākya people, in or near Lumbini in what is now Nepal. His father, Suddhodana, led the clan. The Śākyas were a small oligarchic republic rather than a kingdom, which already sits awkwardly with the "prince in a palace" image. Even his dates are unsettled. Traditional reckoning gives roughly 563–483 BCE; a good deal of modern scholarship prefers a later window, closer to 480–400 BCE. A century of uncertainty about someone this significant is a useful reminder of how thin the ground is. What we have is the Pali Canon, written down in Sri Lanka around the first century BCE after generations of careful oral transmission, along with parallel collections preserved in Chinese and Sanskrit. Where those independent lines agree, we are on reasonably firm ground. Where a story appears only in later commentary, it is later commentary — which is not the same as false, but is worth knowing. The four sights, and where they come from The famous version: a sheltered prince, kept from all suffering, ventures out and encounters an old man, a sick man, a corpse, and a wandering ascetic — and leaves that night. It is a superb piece of storytelling, and in that fully-developed form it belongs to later biographical literature, principally the Nidānakathā commentary, composed many centuries after his death. The earliest texts are quieter and, to my ear, more affecting. In one discourse he simply describes noticing that he was himself subject to ageing, sickness and death, and that this made his own comfort feel hollow. There is no dramatic outing. There is a young man of some privilege who registers a fact everybody knows and is unable to un-notice it. The legend has him shocked by the discovery of suffering. The mistakes do not vary. What follows is the list I keep in my head: what each habit is, why it feels like the responsible choice while you are doing it, what it actually costs, and the specific different action to take instead. This one is about the mentee, and it is the harder of the two to write, because none of these mistakes look like mistakes from inside. pages.d: The rules you were taught — mixed characters, 90-day expiry, never paste — are now recommended against by the bodies that gave them to us.
pages.b: Password advice that stopped being true Security The password advice that stopped being true Mix upper case, lower case, a digit and a symbol. Change it every ninety days. Never paste it in. Three of those rules are now formally recommended against by the same bodies that gave them to us, and the man who wrote the original guidance has said publicly that he regrets it. Here is what changed, who changed it, why each rule failed, and what is actually true now. Published 31 August 2026 · 10 min read · by Krunalkumar Shah Where the old rules came from Almost everyone reading this was taught the same four things about passwords. Mix upper case, lower case, a digit and a symbol. Change it every ninety days. Never write it down. Never paste it in. Three of those are now formally recommended against by the standards bodies that popularised them, and the fourth has been reversed in spirit. Named people changed them, in named documents, for stated reasons — and the reasons are more useful than the rules. The composition rules came from NIST Special Publication 800-63, published in 2003, and specifically from its Appendix A on estimating password strength. That appendix was written by Bill Burr, then a manager at NIST. It was not careless work. It was work done with almost no real password data — nobody published corpuses of real credentials in 2003 — leaning instead on older research into how guessing worked on mainframes. The advice followed logically from its model of attacker behaviour. The model was what turned out to be wrong. In 2017 Burr told the Wall Street Journal that he regretted much of it; the line reported was “Much of what I did I now regret.” That is not a gotcha. It is a researcher publicly marking his own work as superseded, which is what you want from the people who write standards, and which rarely gets heard. What NIST says now The reversal lives in NIST SP 800-63B, Digital Identity Guidelines: Authentication and Lifecycle Management . Its section on memorised secrets — NIST’s term for passwords — is short and unusually blunt. Paraphrasing what changed most: No composition rules. Do not demand particular mixes of character types. No arbitrary expiry. No periodic forced changes — but a forced change is required on evidence of compromise. Allow long secrets. pages.b: The Real Cost of a Manual Process Business The real cost of a manual process Almost every automation argument I have watched go badly went badly at the same moment: somebody said the manual way was costing too much time, somebody else said it was fine, and nobody had a number. It is a real feeling, and it is usually pointing at something true, but it cannot be argued with and it cannot be compared. Two people can hold it about two different processes and there is no way to tell which one to fix first. Worse, the opposite feeling — "it only takes a minute" — is equally unfalsifiable, and it wins more arguments than it should, because a minute genuinely does sound like nothing. The fix is not sophistication. It is arithmetic that a person can do on paper and that anybody in the room can check. What follows is deliberately simple: I would rather have a number that is roughly right and openly assumption-marked than a spreadsheet with fourteen tabs that nobody trusts and nobody can audit. Published 22 August 2026 · Updated 27 August 2026 · 6 min read · by Krunalkumar Shah How the trick is staged Search for a resume builder and the top results all open the same way: a clean editor, a row of templates, a live preview, and no price anywhere on the page. You pick a template and start typing. Name, phone, email, city. Every employer you've had, with dates. Education. Skills. Thirty to sixty minutes of honest work, and the preview looks genuinely good — that part is real, the editors are usually well built. Then you click Download , and the product reveals itself. First a sign-up wall — the document you just wrote is held behind an account. Then the actual mechanism, which comes in two flavours: a PDF with a watermark across your work history, or a checkout page. Often the checkout is a "trial" for a small amount that quietly renews at a much larger monthly rate, with the cancellation path buried somewhere in an account settings page you will visit exactly once, angry, three months from now. The price was never missing. It was scheduled — for the exact moment your cost of walking away is highest. That timing is the whole design. Before you typed anything, the honest comparison was "this site versus any other site." After an hour of data entry it is "pay a few hundred rupees versus retype everything somewhere else," and the sunk cost does the selling. None of this is illegal — the terms are disclosed, technically, somewhere — but it is a textbook dark pattern: the interface is engineered so you commit before you can evaluate. pages.b: Types of Cyberattacks & the CIA Triad Security Types of cyberattacks, mapped: causes, defenses, and the CIA triad Every attack you have ever read about — phishing, ransomware, DDoS, SQL injection — breaks one of just three promises a system makes. This is the map I wish someone had drawn for me: six attack families, why each one keeps working, and where prevention ends and mitigation begins. Published 10 August 2026 · 13 min read · by Krunalkumar Shah The three promises every attack breaks Security has a reputation for being endless — new attack names every week, each sounding like its own specialty. But underneath the naming noise, every attack is trying to break one of exactly three promises. Security professionals call them the CIA triad : Confidentiality — only the right people can see the data. Broken when secrets leak: stolen customer records, read email, exposed credentials. Integrity — the data and the system are what they claim to be. Broken when something is altered: a tampered invoice, a poisoned software update, a defaced site. Availability — the system works when legitimate users need it. Broken when service stops: a flooded server, an encrypted disk, a frozen machine. This lens is the whole trick. Ask "which promise does this attack break?" and an unfamiliar attack stops being scary vocabulary and becomes a variation of something you already understand. Ransomware is primarily an availability attack that uses malware. Phishing is usually a confidentiality attack that goes through a person instead of a computer. My own research subject — the humble fork bomb — is a pure availability attack made of nothing but permitted actions. Attackers don't respect category boundaries, and real incidents chain several types together. The categories aren't for the attacker's benefit — they're for yours, because each family falls to the same kinds of defense. The map: six attack families Here is the landscape in one picture. Six families, grouped by how the attack works — through people, code, networks, load, applications, or logins — with the promise each one usually breaks. pages.b: Types of Love, and Choosing Someone to Marry Life Types of love, and choosing someone to marry English gives us one word for the feeling you have about your mother, your closest friend, someone you met three weeks ago, and a plate of food. That is partly true and partly a modern tidying-up — the ancient usage was messier than the lists suggest, and the popular "six types" framing owes a lot to the psychologist John Alan Lee, writing in the 1970s. Still, the distinctions are genuinely useful, whatever their provenance: Eros — desire and passion. Intense, physical, and by its nature not constant. Philia — deep friendship. Respect, shared interests, enjoying someone's company for its own sake. Storge — the steady affection of family. Unglamorous, and it survives things the others do not. Pragma — a settled, practical love built over long partnership. Compromise, patience, shared logistics. Agape — love that expects nothing back. Philautia — regard for yourself. Healthy in one form, corrosive in another. The practical point: a marriage that lasts usually needs at least three of these running at once, and the one that gets all the attention in films — eros — is the one least able to hold weight on its own. pages.d: A UPI collect request and a payment look almost identical on screen, and only one takes money. The six scripts, and what to do in the first hour.
pages.b: UPI Fraud: How the Money Leaves Security UPI fraud: how the money actually leaves A request for money and an offer of money look almost the same on a phone screen, and one of them takes while the other gives. Nearly every UPI fraud in India lives inside that resemblance. This is the mechanism, written to be forwarded to a parent, and the one sentence in it is worth more than the rest of the article put together. Published 31 August 2026 · 21 min read · by Krunalkumar Shah The one sentence worth forwarding If you send one line from this page to somebody, send this one: The UPI PIN authorises money leaving your account. Always. No refund, no cashback, no prize, no salary arrear, no insurance payout and no returned wrong transfer has ever required you to enter it. That is the whole defence, and it is short enough to say down a phone line. Everything else in this article is the reasoning behind it, the shapes the lie arrives in, and what to do when it has already worked. I have volunteered as a registered cyber-expert supporting law enforcement since 2020, and the cases that reach me are almost never technical. They converge on a single moment: somebody who genuinely believed money was about to arrive typed six digits that sent it instead. Nothing was broken into. No password was guessed. The person authorised their own debit, because the screen in front of them was describing a different transaction from the one it was about to perform. Two screens that are not the same Open any UPI app and look at what a collect request actually renders as. There is a name at the top, a UPI ID under it, a note, an amount, and a bar across the bottom. Now look at a payment you are about to make. Name, ID, note, amount, bar across the bottom. They are the same card. The difference is which text on that card the other party controls, and it is nearly all of it. The display name is whatever their account is registered as, which can read CUSTOMER CARE — REFUND DESK . The note is free text they typed, which can read approve to receive your refund . The amount is chosen by them. None of it is verified as a description of what the screen will do, because none of it is a field the payment system inspects — it is a label being carried along. There is exactly one line on the screen the other party cannot write, and it is the bar at the bottom. Your app writes that line, and it says pay . No ads, no accounts, nothing to install. A fair question is what any of that is doing on a consultant's website. Part of the answer is that nine of them are security games. One deals you twenty emails and texts, half of them genuine, and makes you call each one — phishing practice with the reason given the moment you answer. Another lets you type a password and watch a real cracking run go after it: wordlist first, then mangling rules, then brute force . People who will not read a paragraph about password hygiene will happily lose to that game three times in a row, and the lesson survives in a way the paragraph never does. Play is the oldest teaching technology there is. But the honest answer is the other one: building the games taught me more than building the serious pages did. A game is ordinary software with the difficulty turned up — real-time input, persistent state, an impatient user — and none of the forgiveness. Nobody files a bug report against a marketing page. Everyone notices when Pac-Man eats a ghost he has no right to eat. Every bug in this article is real. Each one shipped, was caught by the adversarial review this site's build depends on, and is fixed now. What makes them worth writing about is that none of them is really a game bug. Each is a production bug class, caught small. pages.b: What a Marriage Biodata Leaks Security What a marriage biodata leaks No other document an Indian family shares as casually carries as much identity as a marriage biodata: date and place of birth, mother's name, home address, income, and a photograph — one A4 page, forwarded to people you have never met. This is that page read the way an attacker reads it, and the sharing hygiene that costs nothing. Published 22 August 2026 · Updated 27 August 2026 · 5 min read · by Krunalkumar Shah One page, read as an attacker reads it Lay a typical biodata on the table and inventory it the way you would audit a system. Full legal name. Date of birth — and usually the time and place of birth too, because horoscope matching wants them. Father's full name, mother's full name. The complete home address. Height, and the education line. Employer, designation, and an income figure stated to the rupee. Sibling names and what they do. A phone number, and a photograph, usually taken at home on a phone. I recently wrote about what resume builders do with your work history , and a resume is genuinely the milder sibling of this document. A resume tells a stranger where you worked. A biodata tells them who your mother is, where you sleep, what you earn, and when and where you were born — and then it gets forwarded through WhatsApp groups and matrimonial brokers to an audience nobody is keeping a list of. The document is not the problem; the fact that nobody treats it as sensitive is. Half the page is account-recovery answers Look at the classic identity-verification questions still used by banks, telecom operators, and older account-recovery flows: date of birth, place of birth, mother's maiden name. Now look at the biodata again — it answers all three, in print, above a photograph. Security people call this knowledge-based authentication, and it fails precisely when the "knowledge" has been shared; a biodata shares it with every household and broker in the chain. The same fields are the skeleton of a convincing "verification call." A caller who opens with your full name, date of birth, father's name, and address does not sound like a stranger — and that credibility is the raw material for SIM-swap attempts and bank social engineering. None of this means a biodata causes identity theft. It means the page is a pre-filled answer sheet, and the only remaining question is who ends up holding a copy.
