pages.b: What a Security Review Actually Finds Business What a security review actually finds People want to know what a review will turn up before they agree to one, which is fair. The honest answer is that it is usually the same short list, in roughly the same order, for reasons that are almost never carelessness. Here is that list, the difference between a review and the two things it gets confused with, and the part that does not belong on a sales page: a clean review does not mean you are secure. Published 31 August 2026 · 20 min read · by Krunalkumar Shah What a review actually is A security review is a structured read of a system by somebody who did not build it, with access to everything: the source, the configuration, the cloud console, the deployment pipeline, and an hour with the engineers. It is time-boxed. Its job is to enumerate the ways the system can be made to do something it should not, work out which of those an attacker would actually reach, and hand back an ordered list of changes. The access is the whole point. On a small product, reading is enormously more efficient than guessing. An outsider probing a login form from the internet has to infer what the code does; a reviewer with the repository open can see the handler that forgot a check, and can see it in ten minutes rather than two days. The trade-off is that a reviewer with full access is not proving the attacker's path — that is a different exercise, and it is the next section. A review is also not a scan. Automated tooling is one input among several, and on the systems I see it produces two useful findings and four hundred lines of noise. The value a person adds is deciding which of those four hundred lines is reachable from the request path, and noticing the thing no scanner has a rule for, which is nearly always the authorisation logic. Review, penetration test, red team Clients routinely ask for one of these and need another. The words are used loosely across the industry, including by people selling them, so it is worth being exact. A review is white box and broad. You hand over everything and I read it. The output is a ranked list of weaknesses with the smallest change that closes each one. It is the right first engagement for a product nobody outside the team has ever looked at, because it finds the most per unit of money and it finds things that are invisible from the outside. pages.h: What “AI agent” means once you have to maintain one
pages.d: The word covers everything from one tool call to a swarm of loops. The honest spectrum, and what really changes once you have to maintain one.
pages.b: AI agents, once you maintain one AI engineering What “AI agent” means once you have to maintain one “Agent” has stopped meaning anything specific. It covers a single prompt with one tool call, and it covers a swarm of coordinating loops, which makes it useless for deciding what you are about to build. The definition that matters is the one you arrive at six months later, when you are the person keeping the thing running. Published 31 August 2026 · 10 min read · by Krunalkumar Shah I build automation for a living, so I get sent a lot of things described as agents. Most of them are not, in the sense the word is being sold. Some should not be, and are better for it. The spectrum the word hides The word is doing at least five jobs at once, ordered here by how much control you hand over: A prompt with a tool call. One model call that may come back asking you to run a function. You run it, hand the result back, done. No loop. A fixed chain. Steps in a known order: pull the record, classify it, draft a reply, queue it. The control flow is yours and identical on every run. A router. The model picks one branch of several and each branch is ordinary code. The only non-deterministic decision is which branch, testable on its own. A loop with tools and a stopping condition. The model decides what to do next, repeatedly, until something stops it. This is what most people mean, and where every problem below starts. A multi-agent system. Several of those loops talking to each other. Everything below, multiplied, plus a new failure mode: two loops can be confidently wrong at each other. Most things sold as agents are the second or the third, and that is usually right. A fixed chain is inspectable, its cost is knowable before you run it, and it breaks in the same place twice. What would change my mind: if the next step genuinely depends on what the last one returned, in a way you cannot enumerate in advance, the loop earns its keep. If you can draw the flowchart, you do not need a system that invents it at runtime. From here, “agent” means the fourth item; for the tool landscape itself, which AI tool for which job is the map. Your test suite is a distribution, not a pass or a fail Ordinary software gives the same output for the same input, so a test can assert equality and mean it. An agent gives you a distribution . What the person means is: when our assessor asks how we satisfy the awareness requirement, will this hold up? Those are two different questions, and only one of them is about the trainer. This is what the standards actually say, what an assessor asks to see, and what nobody can promise you. Published 31 August 2026 · 17 min read · by Krunalkumar Shah The question behind the question "Is your training certified?" is a question about the vendor. "Will this satisfy our auditor?" is a question about your file. They get asked in the same breath and they have almost nothing to do with each other, which is why the conversation so often ends with both sides slightly disappointed. No logo on a certificate satisfies an awareness control. What satisfies it is a record showing that the right people were trained on the right things at the right time, inside a programme somebody planned. Most of that record is produced by you, not by whoever stands at the front of the room. The trainer contributes four artefacts and a date. You contribute the plan, the personnel list, the follow-up for the people who missed it, and the discipline to keep all of it in one place. So the useful version of this article is not "book me." It is: here is what each of the three regimes you are most likely to be facing actually asks for, here is the pack that answers it, and here is the line past which no training vendor — including this one — can help you. What this is and is not. This is practitioner orientation from someone who builds and delivers the material, not legal advice and not an assurance opinion. Standards get revised, rules get notified, and your own assessor's judgement governs your engagement. pages.d: What India's DPDP Act 2023 actually requires of a small company: the consent standard, the notice and its languages, the rights, and the penalty schedule.
pages.b: What Consent Actually Means Under DPDP Security What consent actually means under the DPDP Act India's data protection law hands an ordinary business two ways to make processing lawful, and one of them is a short closed list that probably does not cover you. Everything else runs on consent — and the Act is specific about what consent is, who has to prove it, and what happens when someone takes it back. This is that law read as an engineering problem, by somebody who has to make systems satisfy it rather than argue about it in court. Published 31 August 2026 · 32 min read · by Krunalkumar Shah What this is and is not. I am a security practitioner, not a lawyer, and nothing here is legal advice. What follows is the reading I use when I have to build or review a system that will be judged against this law: what the statute says, which parts depend on Rules that are still phasing in, and where the engineering work actually is. If you hold a lot of personal data, operate in a regulated sector, or have already had an incident, take advice from someone who can be on the record for it. Dates and figures below are as at 31 August 2026, and the parts that live in the Rules are the parts most likely to have moved since. Why the Act hangs on consent The Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 is a deliberately short statute. You can read the whole thing in an evening, which is not something you can say about the European regulation it is compared to, and the brevity comes from a specific design decision: it does not offer a menu of lawful bases. Europe gives a controller six grounds to choose from, and in practice most commercial processing there runs on two of them — necessity for a contract, and legitimate interests — with consent used sparingly for the awkward cases. India inverted that. Under DPDP, processing is lawful if you have consent, or if it falls inside a closed list the Act calls legitimate uses . There is no legitimate-interests ground. There is no contract-necessity ground. The closed list is genuinely closed, and for a private company running an ordinary business, most of it does not apply. That single structural fact is what makes this post necessary. Consent stops being the fallback and becomes the load-bearing wall. If your consent is defective, the processing built on it is not merely badly documented — it is unlawful, along with everything downstream that depended on it. And the burden of showing you had valid consent sits on you, not on the pe

pages.h: What deepfake detection can and cannot do
pages.d: Why an AI detector's confidence percentage is not evidence, what a forensic examiner actually looks at, and what C2PA provenance genuinely fixes.
pages.b: What Deepfake Detection Can and Cannot Do Security What deepfake detection can and cannot do People send me a video and ask whether it is real. They expect the answer to come from a tool, and they expect the tool to return a number. Neither of those expectations survives contact with the work. Detection is the losing side of an arms race it cannot win by design, and the honest response is not a better detector — it is provenance, and it is process. Published 31 August 2026 · 25 min read · by Krunalkumar Shah The question, and the honest answer The request always arrives in the same shape. A forwarded clip, a screenshot of a screenshot, a voice note that sounds like someone's managing director, and one sentence: can you check if this is real? The person asking wants a yes or a no, and they would settle for a number. I cannot give them one from the file, and neither can anybody else. That is not modesty about my own equipment. It is a statement about what these techniques measure. Every signal a forensic examiner reads from an image or a video measures processing history — what encoders touched this file, how many times, and whether one region of it has a different history from its neighbours. None of them measure truthfulness. A photograph of a real event that has been cropped, resized and sent through two chat apps lights up every one of them. A carefully made fake, saved once through the same chat app, puts them all out. So this article does two things. First it takes apart the promise that a detector can settle the question, because that promise is the reason people stop looking for the answers that would actually have worked. Then it describes what does work, in the two places where it matters: signed provenance for the files that carry it, and process for the situation where a fake is about to cost you money. The uncomfortable structure of this field: the tools that give you a confident answer are the ones you should not trust, and the tools you should trust will not give you a confident answer. Everything in this article is a tool you can run. There is a media forensics lab on this site that takes a photo or a short video and runs the signal set an examiner would look at — provenance, error level analysis, quantisation tables, the noise floor, a frequency plot, copy-move — and says in plain words what each one does and does not imply. pages.d: What the major traditions actually claim about death, where they disagree, what near-death experiences do and do not show, and living with an open question.
pages.b: What Happens After We Die Life What happens after we die This is the one question every tradition has taken a position on and none has settled. I am not going to pretend to an answer. What I can do is set out honestly what the main views actually claim — including where they contradict each other in ways that usually get glossed over — and what the evidence does and does not support. Published 27 August 2026 · 10 min read · by Krunalkumar Shah Why the question will not go away Every human culture we know of has developed elaborate beliefs and rituals around death. That universality is sometimes offered as evidence that something is there, and sometimes as evidence that we are simply built to find the alternative unbearable. Both readings are available and neither is decisive. What is certain is that the question is not idle. How you answer it shapes how you spend a life — what you fear, what you are willing to endure, what you consider worth doing. It deserves better than either confident dismissal or confident assertion. What happens to the body This part is not disputed. Circulation stops, oxygen delivery to tissue ends, and cells begin to fail — neurons within minutes, other tissues over hours. Electrical activity in the brain ceases. Decomposition begins. The disagreement is entirely about whether that is a description of the whole event or only of its physical component. Everything below turns on that single question. The materialist answer On this view, consciousness is something the brain does , in the way digestion is something the stomach does. When the organ stops, the process stops. There is no one left to experience absence, so there is nothing it is like to be dead. The supporting evidence is real and cumulative: damage to specific brain regions reliably alters specific aspects of personality, memory and perception. Anaesthesia interrupts experience entirely. Nothing we have found so far requires anything beyond the physical to explain. The honest gap is that we do not have an account of why physical processes produce subjective experience at all — the "hard problem". That is a genuine open question in philosophy of mind. It is not, by itself, evidence for survival, but anyone claiming the matter is fully closed is overstating. Rebirth: two views that are not the same These get flattened together constantly, including in India where both are ambient. They differ on the point that matters most. pages.b: Your accounts after you die Practical security What happens to your accounts when you die This is the practical companion to a reflective post I wrote about the same subject. Nothing here is unresolved — it is all admin, and all of it lands on someone who is grieving. The problem in one sentence: your accounts are secured against exactly the people who will need them, and every measure you took to keep strangers out works just as well against your family. Published 31 August 2026 · 10 min read · by Krunalkumar Shah The practical half of the same question I wrote a reflective piece about what happens after we die — the question every tradition has answered and none has settled. This is its practical companion, and the opposite kind of writing. Nothing here is unresolved. It is all admin, and it lands on someone who is grieving. The core problem fits in a sentence. Your accounts are secured against exactly the people who will need them. Every measure you took to keep strangers out works identically well against your family, because the system cannot tell the difference — and that indifference is the point of the design, not a bug in it. The classic version is the phone. Two-factor codes arrive on a handset, the handset needs the SIM, and cancelling the mobile number is one of the first tidy administrative jobs a family does. The moment it is deactivated, every account whose recovery runs through SMS becomes unrecoverable, and nobody in the room realises what they have just done. The fragility that makes a number attackable — see how a SIM swap works — makes it a poor inheritance path. It is a bearer token held by an operator, not by you. There is no clean answer. A dormant line costs money and operators eventually recycle released numbers. The narrow advice: do not cancel it in the first week, and move what matters off SMS long before any of this is relevant. What the platforms actually give a survivor Several large providers offer something you can set up in advance. The shared shape matters: almost none of them hand over the account. They hand over a copy of selected data, under conditions, to a person you named while you were alive. Google Inactive Account Manager You choose how long the account has to sit unused before Google concludes something is wrong. It tries to reach you first. They ask it afterwards, with their heart going, and the honest answer starts by refusing the question as asked: opening the page, typing a password, approving a prompt, downloading a file and running it are five different things, and only some of them are serious. Here is what each one actually does, and what to do in the first thirty minutes. They read it afterwards, usually within about ninety seconds, and the question is always the same three words: am I hacked? The honest answer starts by taking the question apart, because "I clicked" describes at least six different events and only three of them need anything done in a hurry. Most writing on this subject answers a question nobody asked — how to spot a phishing email — which is excellent advice arriving several minutes too late. The panic is also usually mis-aimed. Getting those the right way round is most of the value here. Everything turns on one boundary: nothing you did not type, and nothing that did not execute, has cost you anything yet. pages.t: What Is a Fork Bomb in Linux?
pages.h: What is a fork bomb, and why can it freeze a Linux system?
pages.d: How one line of Bash can freeze a hardened Linux system, why ulimit and blacklists fall short, and the smarter defense from my research.
pages.b: What Is a Fork Bomb in Linux? Linux security What is a fork bomb, and why can it freeze a Linux system? One short line of Bash can bring a healthy Linux machine to its knees — no exploit, no special privileges, nothing that looks like an attack. This is how it works, why the usual defenses aren't enough, and the approach I proposed in my research to handle it more gracefully. Published 27 May 2026 · 5 min read · by Krunalkumar Shah Run it yourself, safely. There is a real Linux machine on this site that boots inside your browser with a hard 64 MB ceiling. A fork bomb in there does exactly what this article describes and costs you nothing but a reboot. One catch worth knowing: that shell is BusyBox ash , which rejects the famous :(){ :|:& };: with bad function name — use f(){ f|f& };f instead. Same bomb, one character of difference. Open the Linux terminal The one-liner that does the damage The classic Bash fork bomb is famous for how little it takes: Warning — do not run this. Pasting this into a shell will freeze your machine almost instantly, even inside many VMs, and you'll need a hard reboot. Read on to understand it instead. :(){ :|:& };: It defines a function called : that calls itself twice and pipes one copy into the other, running both in the background — then invokes it. Each process immediately creates two more, which each create two more, and so on. There is no upper limit written anywhere. It is exponential growth with no brake pedal. The unsettling part isn't the cleverness of the code. It's that every individual action it takes is completely legitimate. Creating a process is something any user is allowed to do. Why "just one more process" ends the system Every running program on Linux is a process, and the kernel tracks each one in a finite structure called the process table. Processes also consume memory and CPU scheduling slots. A fork bomb doesn't break any single one of these — it exhausts all of them at once. The process table fills, memory runs out, and the scheduler is so busy juggling a flood of near-identical processes that legitimate work never gets a turn. The result is a machine that hasn't crashed and hasn't been hacked in any traditional sense — it is simply too busy multiplying to respond to you. In security terms, this is an attack on availability , one of the three pillars of information security alongside confidentiality and integrity. pages.h: What running an internship cohort is teaching me about mentorship
pages.d: Why small cohorts beat crowds, hiring for hunger over resumes, giving real work instead of exercises, and why mentorship is mostly restraint.
pages.b: Lessons from Running an Internship Cohort Mentorship What running an internship cohort is teaching me about mentorship When I started mentoring, I assumed the hard part would be teaching. It wasn't. The hard part was everything around the teaching — picking the right people, designing work that actually matters, and learning when to step back. Most of these lessons come from years of mentoring interns and engineers; running my own cohort now is testing every one of them. Published 2 July 2026 · 5 min read · by Krunalkumar Shah A crowd is not a cohort The first thing I got wrong was thinking bigger was better. More applicants felt like success. But a mentorship group is not an audience — it is a working team, and teams have a size beyond which the magic disappears. Past a handful of people you stop mentoring individuals and start broadcasting to a room. Questions go unanswered, quieter people vanish, and the whole thing flattens into a lecture. So I keep my free cohort deliberately small — two or three seats. Not because demand is low, but because attention is finite. I would rather change three careers than entertain thirty inboxes. Small enough that I remember what each person is stuck on without checking my notes; that is the right size. Select for hunger, not résumé Early on I over-weighted credentials — grades, the name of the college, a long list of courses. It is the easiest thing to sort on and almost the least useful. Across the interns and mentees I have mentored over the years — and now in my own cohort — the ones who grew fastest were rarely the ones with the shiniest CVs. They were the ones who showed up with a half-broken project they had built on their own, because that told me the one thing a transcript never can: they will do the work when nobody is watching. Now I look for three signals — evidence they have built something unprompted, the ability to describe a problem clearly, and honesty about what they don't yet know. Someone who admits "I haven't learned this yet" and then tells me how they plan to learn it is worth more to me than any confident bluffer. The goal of selection isn't to reward the best past — it's to find the people most likely to do the work now. Tap the diagram to open it full-screen. Give real work, not exercises Nothing kills motivation like busywork that everyone knows is fake. A toy assignment that gets thrown away teaches people that their effort doesn't matter. pages.h: What your browser tells every site you visit
pages.d: Your browser hands every site your address, time zone, screen, cores and GPU without asking. No single value identifies you. The combination usually does.
pages.b: What your browser tells every site Privacy What your browser tells every site you visit None of these values needed a permission prompt, and none of them identifies you on its own. Together they usually do, and unlike a cookie there is nothing for you to clear. Published 31 August 2026 · 10 min read · by Krunalkumar Shah Read your own values first. There is a page on this site that performs every permissionless read described below and prints the answers in one table: your public address, browser string, time zone, core count, GPU and a canvas fingerprint. The rest of this article is easier to follow with your own numbers in front of you. Open the browser leak check What arrives before any script runs The first facts about you arrive before the page has begun thinking about you. They are part of the request itself. Your IP address is the return address on the packets, so it is not optional and not a tracking decision. It says which network you are on — usually your internet provider, or your employer — and roughly where that network is. It does not say your name, your street, or which person in the building is typing. Geolocation databases map address ranges onto places, and in my experience they get the country right far more often than the city, though I have not measured that systematically. Many home connections rotate addresses, so an IP is a weak long-term identifier by itself. User-Agent names your browser, its version, its engine and your operating system, and on a phone often the device. Accept-Language lists the languages you want the page in, which alone often narrows a country. Referer — misspelled in the standard since 1996 and never corrected — says which page sent you, though most browsers now send only the origin across sites. None of this involves JavaScript. Turning scripts off does not turn it off. How a page learns your public address Browsers ship WebRTC so video calls can connect two machines directly, which means each side must discover what address the other would dial — a question put to a public STUN server. A page can open a peer connection to nobody, let the browser gather those candidates, and read the addresses out. No prompt, because the API was designed for calling rather than for asking permission to be called. That is how VPN leak checkers work, and what the leak page does on load. For each one: what it's genuinely good at, what the free tier gives you, and the exact point where free stops being enough. This category moves faster than any blog can keep up with — plans get renamed, free quotas get cut, and new tiers appear every few weeks. Treat the numbers here as the shape of the market, not a quote. Always confirm on the vendor's own pricing page before you pay. Start with the job, not the tool The reason most "best AI tools" lists are useless is that they answer a question nobody asked. You don't have a tool problem. You have a Thursday problem: a deck to build, a hundred emails to triage, a paper to understand, a client demo to record. The tool is downstream of that. So before you open a single pricing page, answer three questions. What is the actual output? A file, a decision, a saved hour? How often does this job come back? Once, or every week? What happens if the output is wrong? A typo you fix, or an email your client reads? Those three answers pick your tool faster than any comparison table, because they tell you whether you need a generalist, a specialist, or an automation — and whether a free tier can carry it. A one-off job that fails harmlessly? Use a free generalist. A weekly job with real stakes? Pay for the specialist. A job that repeats a hundred times a month? Stop shopping for tools and build a workflow. That last one is most of what I do for clients, and it's usually the cheapest answer of the three. The frequency question does most of the work. Most people over-buy on row one and under-build on row three. Tap the diagram to open it full-screen. The all-rounders: chat assistants This is where nearly everyone starts, and for most people one good assistant covers 70% of what they'd otherwise buy five tools for. The honest truth in 2026 is that the top models are close enough that habit and integration matter more than benchmarks . Pick one, learn it properly, and you'll beat someone who hops between four. pages.h: Why I quote fixed price, what it costs me, and when I refuse
pages.d: Fixed price puts the overrun risk on the person who can control it. The case for it, the premium hidden in every quote, and the work I will not quote that way.
pages.b: Why I quote fixed price Business Why I quote fixed price, what it costs me, and when I refuse A fixed price is a promise about a defined thing. That makes it the fairest structure I know when the scope is genuinely fixed, and a trap for both sides when it is not. Here is the case from the client’s side of the table, the part of the bill that is really a risk premium, and the five kinds of work I will not quote this way. Published 31 August 2026 · 10 min read · by Krunalkumar Shah What a fixed price actually buys the client Nearly every engagement I take ends up fixed-price, and my services page says so plainly. I want to argue for that properly, which means starting on the client’s side of the table and only then admitting what the arrangement costs the person doing the quoting. The first thing a fixed price buys is approvability. A number is a thing a person with a budget can say yes to; an hourly rate is not, because a rate is a rate and a hope. Spend is generally approved on totals rather than rates, so an hourly quote has to be converted into a guess before anyone can sign it, and that guess is usually made by whoever has the least information about the work. A fixed price does the conversion at the only table where it can be done honestly. The second thing is quieter, and I suspect it matters more, though I cannot prove it. A fixed price switches off the meter. Under hourly billing every clarifying question the client asks costs them money, so they ask fewer of them — and those questions are how the work becomes correct. When the price is fixed, a call costs the client nothing, and I end up being told more than I would otherwise have been told. The third is that it ends the argument about efficiency before it starts. Nobody has to wonder whether a task took four hours because the problem was hard or because I was slow — a question that cannot be answered from the outside, and that sits in the room all engagement. The overrun risk belongs to whoever can control it Under time and materials, the client carries the cost of every wrong turn I take. If I pick the wrong library, misread the data model, or spend a day learning something I arguably should have known, the meter runs and they pay for it. They have no lever on any of that. They cannot see the wrong turn coming and could not stop it if they could. I hold to a general principle here: put the risk where the control is. pages.t: Is “We Don’t Store Passwords” True?
pages.h: Why “we don’t store your password” is usually false
pages.d: The claim is false as written and true as intended. What a service actually stores, the ladder from plaintext to Argon2, and how to tell from outside.
pages.b: Is “We Don’t Store Passwords” True? Security Why “we don’t store your password” is usually false The sentence is almost always false as stated and almost always true in the sense intended, and the gap between those two readings is where all of the security lives. Here is what is really in the row, how to judge it from outside without any access, and the one design that makes the claim honest. Published 31 August 2026 · 9 min read · by Krunalkumar Shah What the sentence is trying to say Watch the one-way part first. The hash lab computes MD5, SHA-1 and the SHA-2 family in your own tab. Type a password, change one character, and watch the digest change completely — then look for any route back to the input. There is not one. That property is what the whole claim rests on, and it is worth seeing before we take it apart. Open the hash generator Almost every service you use says some version of it. We never store your password. Your password is never stored in plain text. Not even we can see it. It is usually said in good faith, and the thing it points at is real. Read literally, it is also false nearly every time it is written. What they mean is that they store a hash. A hash function takes an input of any length and produces a fixed-length output called a digest. It is deterministic: the same input always produces the same digest. It is spread out: changing one character produces a completely different digest. And a cryptographic hash is built so there is no practical way to run it backwards — given the digest, you cannot compute the input that made it. That is what makes a login possible without the plaintext. You type your password, the server hashes what you typed, and compares the result against the digest it holds. Equal digests mean you almost certainly typed the same string. The server checked your answer without ever having to read it. So the literal reading — there is no column in the users table containing hunter2 — is usually true, and it matters. An engineer running an ad-hoc query sees digests. A backup that walks out of the building contains digests. A support agent who wants to be helpful cannot be. The trouble is the step the sentence skips. A digest is not nothing. It is a deterministic function of your password and of nothing else, it is sitting in their database, and it is precisely the material an attacker needs in order to start guessing. pages.t: Why Your Automation Broke
pages.h: Why your automation broke, and how to build one that fails loudly
pages.d: An automation that ran for a year does not stop for mysterious reasons. The eight causes that account for it, and the guard that catches each one early.
pages.b: Why Your Automation Broke Automation Why your automation broke, and how to build one that fails loudly The sentence that opens almost every one of these conversations is "we didn't change anything." It is usually true, and it is the reason the thing stopped rather than a defence against it. Your workflow was the only part of the arrangement holding still. Here are the eight causes that actually account for it, what each one looks like from the outside — which is normally silence — and the specific guard that catches it. Published 31 August 2026 · 25 min read · by Krunalkumar Shah Nothing on your side changed An automation is not a program you run. It is a standing agreement between several programs you do not control: a trigger owned by one vendor, an authentication token issued by a second, a record shape defined by a third, a schedule kept by a platform, and a network in between that is nobody's in particular. Every one of those pieces is on somebody else's release calendar, with somebody else's opinion about what counts as a breaking change. So "we didn't change anything" is not a defence. It is the diagnosis. The workflow held still while the ground underneath it moved, and the useful question is never what did we break . It is two other questions: what moved, and why did a customer find out before we did. That second question is the one this article is really about. The first half below is a list of what actually moves — eight causes that between them account for nearly everything I have been called in to look at. The second half is the engineering that turns any of them from a three-week silence into a message you get on the morning it happens. If you only have an afternoon, skip to alerting on absence , which is worth more than the other three guards combined. Why the failure is silent Every alarm most teams own is wired to an error. A step throws, the platform catches it, an email goes out, somebody looks. That is a real mechanism and it works — for the failures where something ran. It does nothing at all for the failures where nothing ran. And the most common breakages sit at the edge of the workflow rather than in the middle of it: the trigger that stops polling, the credential that stops being accepted, the schedule that quietly detaches after a platform migration. pages.b: Why Your Phone Feels Hacked Security Why your phone feels hacked, and probably is not The phone runs hot, the battery is gone by four in the afternoon, and an advert turns up for the exact thing you were talking about at lunch. This is the question I am asked more than any other, by people who are not in security and who are usually being brushed off or frightened rather than answered. So: what is actually causing each of those, the six signals that would change my mind, the checks you can run yourself in twenty minutes, and the part about stalkerware where the safety advice comes before the technical advice. Published 31 August 2026 · 24 min read · by Krunalkumar Shah The question I get most Of everything an ordinary person brings to somebody who works in security, this arrives most often, and it usually arrives sideways — at the end of a call about something else, or as a message that opens with an apology for asking. It comes from relatives, from a client's office manager, from people who found this site looking for something else entirely. The phone is behaving strangely and they want to know whether somebody is in it. There are two standard answers and both are bad. The first is the shrug: phones get hot, you are imagining it, buy a new one. That is comfortable to give and it is wrong often enough to matter, because sometimes the person is right and there is a real signal underneath the noise. The second is the upsell: you may well be infected, here is a scanner, here is a subscription. That answer sells anxiety back to the person who arrived carrying it. The useful answer is a triage, and it starts with a structural fact that reorders everything that follows. When something has genuinely gone wrong, it is far more often the accounts than the device . Compromising a modern phone at the operating-system level is difficult and expensive; it is done, but it is done to specific people for specific reasons. Adding a forwarding rule to a mailbox costs an attacker nothing beyond a password somebody reused. So the checks in this article run in that order — accounts first, phone second — which is the opposite of where everybody's attention naturally goes. I cannot tell you your phone is fine. I have not seen it, and anyone who declares a device clean from a description is guessing. pages.b: Colophon — How This Site Is Built Colophon How this site is built A colophon is the note at the back of a book saying how it was made — the typeface, the paper, the press. This is that note for this site: what it runs on, what it deliberately does without, and why. Every number on this page is counted at deploy time rather than typed, so none of it can quietly go out of date. By the numbers What is actually here 183 HTML pages 62 browser labs 66 games 25 articles 0 dependencies 166 scripts, all mine 165 commits Counted on 2026-08-28 . The stack Hand-written HTML, and very little else There is no framework here, no bundler and no build step in the usual sense. Every page is an .html file you could open in a text editor, and the file you see in the repository is the file the browser is served. package.json exists to name two scripts and a Node version floor; it has 0 dependencies , and nothing generated is committed. That is a constraint rather than a boast. A site that outlives its framework is a site you can still change in five years, and most of what a framework buys you at this size is a rebuild you have to keep working. Runs on Static HTML, CSS and vanilla JavaScript. Vercel for hosting, with clean URLs and security headers set in vercel.json . Does without No framework, no bundler, no CSS preprocessor, no npm packages, and no cookie banner. Three measurement scripts run, all named in the privacy policy : one Google Analytics tag, Vercel Speed Insights, which times how fast the page rendered, and Vercel Web Analytics, which counts pageviews. Neither Vercel script sets a cookie. Runs in your browser The labs execute real language runtimes on WebAssembly locally, and nothing you type or drop into them is uploaded. The handful that look something up on the internet — DNS, RDAP, certificate transparency, breach and email-security checks — say so on the page and ask before they send anything. The privacy policy lists which, and to whom. The deploy A build that is allowed to say no Pushing to main runs one script in a throwaway container. pages.t: A Still Place — Sit for a Moment
pages.h: A still place — sit for a moment
pages.d: A still page. A seated Buddha at dawn, a verse from the Pali Canon that changes each time you come, and a slow breath to follow. Stay as long as you like.
pages.b: A Still Place — Sit for a Moment A still place — sit for a moment As a deep lake is clear and still, so the wise grow calm on hearing the teaching. Dhammapada 82 Another verse The figure and the light around him swell and settle to pace your breathing: breathe in for four seconds as they grow, and out for six as they settle. It repeats until you leave. Breathe in Why this page exists The rest of this site is compilers, packet captures and security write-ups. This one is not. It is here because a page can be a quiet room, and quiet rooms are in short supply. Every verse shown here is from the Pali Canon, with its citation attached. That matters more than it might seem: a great many sayings passed around as the Buddha’s were never his. “Holding on to anger is like grasping a hot coal”, “what you think, you become”, “peace comes from within” — all modern inventions. If a line is worth sitting with, it is worth being honest about where it came from. There are 684 verses here, drawn from ten collections — among them the Dhammapada, the Udāna and Itivuttaka, the Sutta Nipāta, the verses of the senior monks and nuns, and the Saṁyutta Nikāya. You are unlikely to meet the same one twice in a sitting. About 279 of these translations are by Bhikkhu Sujato , published by SuttaCentral and dedicated to the public domain under CC0 ; the verses of the senior monks and nuns were translated by Bhikkhu Sujato and Jessica Walton. Thanks are owed to them, and to SuttaCentral for making the canon freely reusable. The remaining 405, an older set, came from several translators whose names were not recorded at the time — each is cited to chapter and verse and can be checked, but if you hold rights in any of them, please write to me and I will credit or replace it. There is nothing to sign up for and nothing being counted. Stay as long as you like. ← Back to the rest of the site

pages.t: aafire — The ASCII Fire Effect, Free In Your Browser
pages.d: The aalib fire demo in a terminal grid. A heat buffer, one averaging pass a frame, and a ramp of characters. Wind and intensity controls, no score.
pages.b: aafire — The ASCII Fire Effect, Free In Your Browser aafire The fire demo from aalib, the library that draws pictures out of characters. Worth knowing: nothing in it rises. Every cell is the average of the cells below it minus a small decay, run once a frame, and the flame is that arithmetic plus ten characters put in the right order. One averaging pass per frame Ten characters, ordered by ink Wind is a weight, not a shift No score, no clock Flame height 0 rows Screen alight 0% Wind Strong left Left Still Right Strong right Intensity Embers Fire Inferno Pause Restart ⛶ The aafire playfield. The game draws here once it starts. New best Ready? 0 Play Play again Resume This one is 78 columns wide — turn your phone sideways and it gets a great deal easier to read. Nothing to do. The two dropdowns are the whole of the controls. Kept on this device: nothing yet Reset this game’s data How the fire is made One pass, upward Two rows of random heat sit below the bottom of the screen. Every frame each cell takes the average of the three cells below it and the one below those, then loses a small random amount. Heat climbs exactly one row per pass and thins as it goes, and that is the whole simulation — no particles, no velocities, no flames as objects. The ramp does the rest The buffer is a field of numbers between nought and one. What makes it read as fire is the ten characters it is mapped onto, ordered by how much of a cell they fill: a full stop, a colon, up through x and S to a hash and a dollar sign. Shuffle that list and the same numbers stop looking like anything at all. Wind is a weight Leaning the fire by sampling an offset column snaps to whole cells, so a light breeze and a gale come out the same. Here the three samples from the row below are weighted 1+w, 1 and 1-w instead. They still sum to four, so the pass stays a true average and the wind moves heat sideways without creating or destroying any. The bed is not re-rolled The source rows keep their values, and only about a quarter of their cells get a new one each frame. Randomise all of them every frame and the averaging smooths the result into a flat orange band; letting hot spots persist for a few frames is what gives them time to climb into tongues. Questions people ask Is this the real aafire? No. It is the same effect written from scratch for a browser. The original is a C program driving aalib, but the arithmetic is the same idea and the character ramp is chosen the same way. Why does the flame sto Is this the real aafire? Why does the flame stop short of the top? Is there anything to do? No. It is the same effect written from scratch for a browser. The original is a C program driving aalib, but the arithmetic is the same idea and the character ramp is chosen the same way. The decay. Each row up costs a fixed slice of heat, so the fire runs out at a predictable height. Inferno lowers the decay far enough that it reaches the ceiling. Change the wind and watch it lean. That is it, which is why this is filed under toys rather than games.

Two rules that point in opposite directions Below the adit it is too dark to take a step, so the lamp has to be lit. The west heading holds firedamp, so a naked flame in it kills you. Neither is a puzzle on its own; together they have exactly one answer, and it is the same answer Humphry Davy found in 1815. The board in the pump chamber states the rule in plain words well before the rule can be fatal, because a death you could not have seen coming is a trick rather than a puzzle. The score is the haul, minus the wandering Each treasure is worth a fixed amount and you keep only what you are carrying when you climb the stile at the end. On top of that you get whatever is left of two hundred moves, so a run that finds the short way round beats one that finds everything the long way. Blowing yourself up scores nothing at all. The mine tells you the answer before it kills you for not having it. Not really. Run it inside the movement loop instead and the aircraft early in the list are measured against positions the rest have not taken yet, so the same two either crash or do not depending on the order they happened to arrive in. That is the kind of bug a player experiences as the game cheating. Landing is a timing problem, not a button Altitude changes one level per sweep and the aircraft moves one square in the same sweep, so a descent has to be started exactly as many squares out as the altitude you are at. Reach zero anywhere except the airport square, on the runway heading, and it is a crash. pages.t: Bastet — Bastard Tetris, The Evil Tetris
pages.d: Bastet — "bastard Tetris" — replaces the random piece bag with a solver that hands you the worst piece every single time. Free, in your browser.
pages.b: Bastet — Bastard Tetris, The Evil Tetris Bastet Federico Poloni’s bastet does one thing differently from Tetris, and it is enough to change the game entirely: instead of dealing pieces at random, it works out which of the seven shapes would hurt you most, and gives you that one. Every time. There is no bad luck here, only intent. The generator is a solver Every piece is your worst Same rules as Tetris otherwise 280 drops simulated per piece Score 0 Best 0 Lines 0 Level 1 Pause Restart ⛶ The Bastet playfield. The game draws here once it starts. New best Ready? 0 Play Play again Resume ← → Move ↑ Rotate ↓ Soft drop Space Hard drop Pad to move and rotate. Tap the board to hard-drop. ↻ ◀ ▶ ▼ Drop Kept on this device: nothing yet Reset this game’s data How it decides what to give you It plays your move for you first For each of the seven shapes it drops every rotation into every column, scores the board that results, and keeps the BEST outcome — because that is what a competent player would find. Then it serves whichever shape’s best outcome is worst. That is 280 simulated drops per piece, which costs nothing and is genuinely adversarial rather than merely unlucky. Play it next to the fair one The Tetris here uses a proper 7-bag: all seven shapes shuffled and dealt, so your worst drought is capped at twelve pieces. Same rules, opposite generators. Playing both is the fastest way to understand that “random” is a design decision rather than a default, and how much of a game lives in it. Questions people ask Is it actually impossible? No. It is very hard. The solver models a decent player rather than a perfect one, and a shape with nowhere at all to go is skipped rather than served — an instant unavoidable loss reads as a broken game, not a cruel one. How is this different from just bad luck? Bad luck is a distribution. This is a search: it evaluates your actual board before choosing. Twenty S-pieces in a row from a random generator is a story; here it is a plan. What is a good score? Far lower than your Tetris score, and that is the point. pages.t: Binary Search Duel — Search, Then Answer
pages.d: Narrow down my number and see the bits each guess wasted, then think of one while I search — and watch the first answer that contradicts an earlier one.
pages.b: Binary Search Duel — Search, Then Answer Binary search duel Four rounds, alternating. In two of them I have written a number down and you hunt for it, with the interval still alive drawn as a bar, the candidates counted, and the cost of every off-centre guess worked out in bits. In the other two the roles swap: you think of a number and answer higher or lower, and I keep the interval your answers imply — so the moment two of them cannot both be true, I can name which two and show you the range they left empty. There is a third mode with no score in it at all, which is the one that reproduces the overflow bug that sat in java.util.Arrays.binarySearch for nine years. Two halves, roles reversed The bits you wasted, per guess An exact cheat detector The 2006 overflow bug, reproduced Round 1 of 4 Probes 0 of 7 Still alive 100 Over par 0 Best — Mode The duel — four rounds The off-by-one trap Range 1 to 50 1 to 100 1 to 1,000 1 to 10,000 Show the midpoint Pause Restart ⛶ New best Ready? 0 Play Play again Resume ← → Move your guess by one, or answer lower and higher ↑ ↓ Move your guess in bigger steps Enter Commit the guess, or say that is the one Type A guess straight into the field, if you would rather Esc Pause Drag along the bar to place your guess — it clamps to the part still alive, so you cannot spend a guess on a number already ruled out — then tap the button underneath, which carries the number you set. In the answering half the three buttons are the whole interface. In the trap, the array cells are tappable and everything reruns the moment you change a setting. Kept on this device: nothing yet Reset this game’s data Why log n is a floor and not a habit One answer is one bit A yes-or-no answer separates the candidates into two groups, so it can at best halve the survivors, and a guess that splits them unevenly halves them by less than that. The exact floor is slightly kinder than the usual log2(n) , because a correct guess ends the round rather than answering it: with k guesses you can separate at most 2^k − 1 values, so par is the smallest k where that reaches n . For 64 candidates that is seven and not six — the sort of off-by-one this game is otherwise about, so it is computed by doubling rather than by rounding a logarithm. None of the four ranges offered is a power of two, so here the two formulas agree. What an off-centre guess actually costs After each guess the page prints two numbers: what the answer was worth, and what the guess could have Is the number chosen before I start guessing? Can I beat par? What counts as cheating in the half where I answer? How is the score worked out, and why is lower better? Does the overflow really happen in JavaScript? Is anything uploaded, or kept? Yes. In the rounds where you search, the number is drawn when the round begins and does not move afterwards. Nothing here adapts to your guesses to keep the game going longer — which is exactly the trick the second half invites you to try on me, and the reason the second half has a checker in it. Yes, by luck. Par is the worst case: it is the number of guesses that is always enough and sometimes necessary. Guess 50 in a range of 1 to 100 and hit it, and you have used one guess for a job that needs seven. The page says so rather than congratulating you, and the score treats any round at or under par as clean, so luck cannot improve your record either. Only an answer that contradicts one you have already given — and it is detected rather than suspected, because the interval your answers imply becomes empty, and an empty interval means no number of any kind would have produced that sequence. Answering to keep the search working as long as possible is not cheating and is not penalised: it is the adversary argument, and the game names it and then finishes in exactly par. It is the guesses you spent over par in the two rounds where you searched, plus two for each contradiction caught in the rounds where you answered. A flawless duel is worth nothing over par, so it shows as "par". The number written to your browser is actually one higher,

pages.t: Birthday Facts — The Day You Were Born, And Every Day Since
pages.d: Enter a date of birth and get the weekday it fell on, your exact age, days alive, your next birthday and your age on seven planets. Nothing is uploaded.
pages.b: Birthday Facts — The Day You Were Born, And Every Day Since Birthday facts Type in a date of birth and this works out the day of the week it fell on, how old you are to the day, and how many days that adds up to. The weekday comes from Zeller’s congruence rather than a table somebody typed up, and every other figure is arithmetic you could check by hand. The date stays in this tab and is not saved anywhere. Weekday from Zeller’s congruence Leap years handled properly Seven planets, real orbital periods Nothing uploaded, nothing saved Born on — Days alive — Pause Restart ⛶ New best Ready? 0 Play Play again Resume Enter Work it out Tap the field to open your phone’s own date picker, then tap Work it out. Kept on this device: nothing yet Reset this game’s data The arithmetic, since that is the whole page The weekday is calculated, not looked up Zeller’s congruence turns a date into a day of the week with a few lines of integer arithmetic. It works by treating January and February as months 13 and 14 of the previous year, which moves the leap day to the end of the year and out of the middle of the sum. The same formula produces the weekday for your next birthday and for the 1,000-day marks, so all the dates on the page agree with each other by construction. Days are counted between UTC midnights Ask a browser for the gap between two local dates and you are asking about a lifetime that may contain a hundred clock changes, each an hour that has to land somewhere. Counting from UTC midnight to UTC midnight avoids the question entirely: those are exactly 86,400 seconds apart, always, so the day count is a subtraction rather than an estimate. “Years, months and days” has to pick a convention Whole months are counted first and the leftover days measured from there, with the month step clamped to the end of a short month — so one month after 31 January is 28 February and the day count restarts on the 28th. Other calculators borrow days from the previous month instead and can differ from this by a day or two around month ends. Neither is wrong; they are answering slightly different questions. The heartbeat figure is a multiplication Days alive, times 24, times 60, times 70. Seventy is the middle of the resting range for an adult and it is the only assumption in the sum. Your real rate ran far higher through childhood and changes every minute of every day, so the number is worth an order of magnitude and nothing more precise than that. Ages on other planets are just di Is the day of the week right for old dates? What if I was born on 29 February? Another calculator gives a different age. Which is right? Is my date of birth sent anywhere? How accurate is the heartbeat number? Why is Pluto not in the table? Back to 1583 it is, on the Gregorian calendar. Earlier than that the form refuses, because the Gregorian calendar arrived in 1582 in some countries, 1752 in Britain and its colonies and 1918 in Russia — so the weekday for a date in 1650 depends on where you are asking about, and one answer would be a guess dressed as a fact. Your age and day counts are exact either way, since they never need an anniversary. For the next birthday in an ordinary year this page uses 1 March; some places use 28 February instead. The result says which it used. Both, probably. The disagreement will be in the months-and-days part, near the end of a short month, and it comes from how each one adds a month to the 29th, 30th or 31st. Total days alive is not a matter of opinion and should match exactly. No. It is typed into a field, used for arithmetic in the same tab, and never leaves it. It is not stored either — no localStorage, no cookie. Reload the page and the field is empty. It is arithmetic, not measurement: days alive times 1,440 minutes times 70 beats. Treat it as the right size rather than the right number. It has not been a planet since 2006. If you want the figure anyway, its orbit is about 90,560 Earth days, so divide your days alive by that.

pages.t: Boids — Flocking Simulation You Can Break, Free In Your Browser
pages.d: Craig Reynolds's flocking model. Separation, alignment and cohesion — three rules per bird, no leader, no plan. Move the sliders and watch the flock fall apart.
pages.b: Boids — Flocking Simulation You Can Break, Free In Your Browser Boids Every bird looks only at its neighbours and follows three rules: do not crowd them, head roughly the way they are heading, and drift toward the middle of them. Nothing knows about the flock — and yet there it is. Turn one rule down and watch what it was holding together. Three rules, no leader Sliders that break it Your cursor is a hawk Hundreds of birds at sixty frames Birds 220 Separation Alignment Cohesion Flock size 80 birds 220 birds 450 birds ∿ Pause Restart ⛶ The Boids playfield. The game draws here once it starts. New best Ready? 0 Play Play again Resume Space Scatter them and start again Move Your cursor scares them Drag on the flock to scare it. The sliders change the three rules. Kept on this device: nothing yet Reset this game’s data How it stays fast Neighbours by bucket, not by brute force Comparing every bird with every other is 200,000 distance checks a frame at 450 birds. Instead each bird is filed into a grid cell the size of its view radius, so it only ever looks at nine cells. That is the difference between sixty frames a second and nine. The colour is the heading Each bird is tinted by the direction it is flying, so the structure of the flock reads as colour as well as position. A flock rotating around a common centre becomes obvious instantly, which it is not when everything is one colour. Questions people ask What happens if I turn separation off? They collapse into a single point and stay there. Separation is the only rule pushing outward, so without it cohesion wins completely. And alignment? You get a milling swarm rather than a flock — they stay together but never agree on a direction. It looks like insects instead of birds. Is this how real flocks work? Broadly, yes. Reynolds proposed it in 1986 as a model rather than a measurement, and later studies of actual starlings found birds do track a small fixed number of neighbours rather than everything they can see. pages.t: Cache Game — A Cache Simulator You Play
pages.d: A real cache simulator. See the tag, index and offset split for every access, pick the evictions yourself, then optimise a loop against Belady optimal.
pages.b: Cache Game — A Cache Simulator You Play Cache game Cache size, block size, associativity and a replacement policy, simulated properly — and the address cut into a tag, an index and an offset in front of you on every single access, because that decomposition is the part nobody quite internalises. On the first four levels you are the cache: the stream comes at you one access at a time and you say which line to throw out. On the last three the cache is fixed and the access pattern is yours to fix instead. Your misses are set beside the policy you chose and beside Belady optimal, which is computed for real by reading the rest of the stream and is therefore the one thing no cache can ever do. Tag, index and offset, every access Belady optimal, computed for real The three Cs counted separately Seven levels, three of them yours to optimise Level 1/7 Hit rate — Misses 0 Score 0 Best — Level 1. Two ways, one choice 2. Where LRU has nothing left 3. Dirty lines cost more 4. Ten blocks, eight lines 5. Row-major or column-major 6. One stride, one set 7. Block the multiply Replacement policy LRU FIFO MRU Random Write-back Step Binary Pause Restart ⛶ New best Ready? 0 Play Play again Resume Space Issue the next access, or take the eviction ← → Move between the lines you may evict ↑ ↓ Move between the patterns you may try Esc Pause Everything is a real button, so nothing needs a drag or a swipe. Tap Step in the toolbar to issue the next access; when a set fills up its lines become buttons and you tap the one to evict. On the last three levels you tap an access pattern to run it, and Step becomes Next level once the target is met. A tap on the board itself does nothing. Kept on this device: nothing yet Reset this game’s data What it simulates, and what it leaves out The three fields are arithmetic, not a heuristic A block of B bytes needs log₂ B offset bits to pick a byte inside it. A cache of S sets needs log₂ S index bits to pick the set, and the set is not a suggestion — a block whose index is 2 may live in set 2 or nowhere. Everything above those two fields is the tag, stored beside the data so a line can say which of the many blocks that share its set it is currently holding. Change the associativity and the number of sets changes, so the boundary between tag and index moves. That is what the toolbar is doing when the split on screen redraws. The processor explorer reports the real cache sizes of the machine you are reading this on. Belady is a bou Is this a real cache from a real processor? How am I allowed to beat LRU? Is Belady cheating? What is the difference between a capacity miss and a conflict miss? Does write-back change the hit rate? What happens if I change the policy or the level halfway through? Is anything stored or sent anywhere? No. The parameters are invented and deliberately tiny — sixty-four to five hundred and twelve bytes, sixteen-bit addresses — so that the whole cache fits on screen and the binary split of an address is short enough to read. The arithmetic is the real thing: an L1 data cache on a current desktop is typically 32 or 48 KB, 64-byte lines and eight to twelve ways, and it computes its index and tag exactly the way this does. Nothing is measured from your machine here; the processor explorer is the page that does that. You are shown the whole access stream, including the part that has not happened yet, and you are allowed to read it. That is the only advantage you have, and it is the same advantage Belady has. A cache has neither. So beating LRU here proves nothing about LRU and everything about how much information a replacement policy is missing — which is the point of putting the two numbers side by side. A capacity miss would have happened even in a perfect cache of that size: the working set is simply bigger than the cache. A conflict miss would not have: the block was thrown out only because the index bits sent it to a set that was already busy, while lines elsewhere sat idle. pages.b: Tech Career Quiz — Which Side Of Technology Suits How You Work Tech career quiz Eighteen questions about the way you like to work and what you find satisfying — never about what you already know, because knowing a thing and wanting to do it all day are unrelated. It scores six tracks: security, backend, frontend, data, infrastructure and product. The result names your top two, describes what the work is actually like, and includes the tedious parts, because those are the bit that decides whether you last. A careers quiz that tests knowledge only tells you what you happen to have studied already, which is mostly an accident of your syllabus. These ask what you would chase for two days, what irritates you, and which tedious job you would mind least. Every track appears in exactly nine questions Eighteen questions, three options each, and each of the six tracks is on offer nine times. That balance is the reason the bars can say something specific: your percentage is how often you picked a track when it was actually available. Without it, whichever track was listed most often would win most quizzes, and the result would be measuring the author. Two tracks, because one is not enough to name a job "Security" on its own covers a penetration tester and a compliance lead, who share almost nothing day to day. The result blends your top two and names the kind of role that sits between them — data plus infrastructure is a platform job, frontend plus product is design engineering, and so on. The tedium is in the write-up on purpose Every track description carries a line about the dull part: the alerts that are nothing, the migrations that must not lose a row, the cleaning that eats most of a data week, the on-call. On a good day these six jobs look fairly similar. On an ordinary one they are miles apart, and that is the difference worth knowing before you pick. pages.b: Firewall Defence — Rules Are The Towers Firewall defence Packets walk down a wire from the internet to your server, each one carrying the only four things a packet filter gets to see: protocol, source address, destination port, and whether it belongs to a connection you already had. You place rules along the wire, they are read in order, and the first one that matches decides. Some of that traffic is an attack and most of it is the business trying to work — and the score is attacks blocked minus legitimate traffic you dropped, so a wall that stops everything finishes several hundred points down. That is the entire point of the game. Across the six waves there are sixty malicious packets and seventy-two legitimate ones, which is why a default-deny policy with no accept rules under it finishes on about minus 264 rather than on a comfortable 600. The opposite mistake is faster: leave everything open and the server takes twenty hits and stops answering, usually somewhere in wave three. Neither of the two policies anyone reaches for first survives this, and that is the argument the whole game is making. First match wins, so wh Why am I losing points for blocking traffic? Blocking a customer costs twelve points and blocking an attack earns ten, so a firewall that refuses everything is scored as the outage it is. This is the one thing the game exists to say: a rule set is judged by what it lets through as much as by what it stops, and the second number is the one nobody puts on a dashboard. Both stop the packet and both score the same here. DROP says nothing at all, so the sender waits for a timeout and learns nothing. REJECT returns an error immediately, which is kinder to a legitimate client that would otherwise hang, and which also confirms to whoever is scanning you that something is there. pages.b: Fireworks — The Bang Arrives After The Flash Fireworks Shells climb on a trail, slow to nothing at the top, and break into a peony, a chrysanthemum trailing sparks, a willow that droops, a crossette that splits again, a ring, or a shell that breaks four times over. Every star is under gravity and drag and burns down from white-hot to a dull ember, and the smoke hangs about afterwards and drifts. The detail the whole thing rests on is the one you cannot see: each report is booked at the distance of its own burst divided by the speed of sound, so the bang lands about half a second after the flash — which is most of the difference between fireworks and moving dots. What separates them is drag and burn time: a peony stops about 105 px out because 100 px/s against a drag of 0.95 goes nowhere further, while a willow is barely slowed at all and burns for three and a half seconds, so gravity has time to pull it into fronds. pages.t: Guess The Algorithm — Name The Sort From Its Animation
pages.d: Six sorting algorithms animated on a bar chart. Name the one running before it finishes — the earlier you call it, the more it is worth.
pages.b: Guess The Algorithm — Name The Sort From Its Animation Guess the algorithm A sort starts running on twenty-four bars and you have twelve seconds to say which one it is. Every run takes the same twelve seconds whatever it costs, so the clock cannot give it away — the giveaway has to be the movement. After each round you get the tell that separates that sort from the ones it is most often confused with. Six sorts, properly implemented Every run is the same length The tell explained each round Nothing is uploaded Round 1/5 Score 0 Worth now — Best 0 Pause Restart ⛶ The Guess the algorithm playfield. Next round Click Name the sort ← → Move between the four names Enter Lock in the highlighted name Tap one of the four names under the chart, then Next round to carry on. Kept on this device: nothing yet Reset this game’s data How to tell six sorts apart Swapped, or overwritten? This is the first question, and it halves the field immediately. Bubble, selection, quicksort and heapsort trade two bars at a time, so heights move around the chart. Insertion and merge sort overwrite positions instead, so bars change height where they stand. Once you can see which of the two is happening you are choosing between three, not six. Which end is filling up Bubble sort and heapsort both build their answer from the right, and people mix them up constantly. The difference is what the left looks like while they do it: bubble sort leaves the unsorted part getting gradually tidier, because every pass nudges everything a little; heapsort leaves it in heap order, which looks like nothing at all. Selection and insertion sort both fill from the left, and there the difference is noise — selection sort scans in silence and swaps once, insertion sort shifts a whole run of neighbours for every element. Recorded first, then replayed ES5 has no generators, and a recursive sort cannot be paused halfway down its own call stack. So each sort here runs to completion the moment the round starts, logging every comparison, swap and write, and the animation replays that log. The algorithms stay textbook rather than being rewritten as state machines to make them pausable. Where to go next This is a recognition drill, not a tutorial. Why only twenty-four bars? How is the score worked out? Yes. Bubble, selection, insertion, merge, quicksort and heapsort are written as they are normally written, and every run is checked to produce a sorted array. Nothing is faked for the animation. The duration does not — every run is stretched or squeezed to the same twelve seconds. The number of steps still differs, so quicksort changes the picture less often than bubble sort does, and you are welcome to use that. It is real information about the cost. Enough for the patterns to be distinguishable, few enough that individual bars are visible on a phone. At two hundred bars everything looks like static and the only thing you can read is the overall shape. pages.t: Incident Response Tabletop — A Breach On A Clock
pages.d: Ransomware and a wire fraud, played over simulated hours. Isolate fast and the evidence goes with it; wait and the attacker moves. Ends in an after-action report.
pages.b: Incident Response Tabletop — A Breach On A Clock Incident response An alert fires at two in the morning and there are four things you could do, none of them free. Isolate the host and the volatile evidence goes with it; wait for more data and the attacker gets another twenty minutes; rebuild before imaging and you can never answer what left the building. Two scenarios — a ransomware outbreak and a wire fraud through a compromised mailbox — each with several branch points, and an after-action report at the end that names what your choices actually cost. Deciding under incomplete information is the skill; the meters are there to show you what you traded for what. Kept on this device: nothing yet Reset this game’s data Why there is no right answer Every choice costs minutes, and so does thinking Each option carries its real cost — a disk image and memory capture is fifty-five minutes, a rebuild from the golden image is eight — and deliberation adds a quarter of a simulated minute for every real second, capped so that reading carefully can never cost more than a quarter of an hour on any one decision. The attacker’s own schedule runs off the same clock, which is why an event can land while you are still reading the options rather than politely between two of them. The Measured pressure setting turns the deliberation clock off entirely and widens the attacker’s timings, for anyone who wants to read at their own pace. An encoding has no key at all — it is only a different way of writing the same characters, and reversing it is a one-click operation that the encoder in the Labs section will happily do for you. Binary, Base64 and ROT13 get mistaken for security constantly, usually by somebody who has just Base64-ed a password into a config file. All that hides it from is a casual glance. Characters and bytes are different counts The two numbers in the bar disagree the moment you leave ASCII. A plain Latin letter is one byte in UTF-8, an accented one is two, most Devanagari characters are three and an emoji is four. That is why a form with a 20-character limit sometimes rejects a name that is plainly shorter than twenty letters: somebody counted bytes and called them characters. Every row is somewhere real Hex is what a memory dump or a hex editor shows you. Base64 is how an image gets into an email or a data: URL. Morse is a telegraph code with no lower case, so anything it cannot carry is dropped and the line under it says how many. ROT13 was a Usenet convention for hiding spoilers. pages.t: Buffer Overflow Puzzle — Four Levels
pages.d: Craft the input that takes the return address on a toy machine. Four levels: the plain overflow, a stack canary, a no-execute stack and a randomised base.
pages.b: Buffer Overflow Puzzle — Four Levels Overflow puzzle A made-up machine with thirty-two cells of memory, a stack that grows down, and a note server with one bad line in it: a copy that has no idea how big the buffer is. Level one is the whole bug — walk your message off the end of an eight-cell buffer and put your own address into the two cells the return instruction reads, with every byte drawn as it lands. Then each level adds one mitigation, in roughly the order the industry added them, and asks you to get past it anyway: a stack canary, a no-execute stack, and a base address that moves every time the process starts. The machine is invented and none of this is a working technique. The picture is the part that transfers. Four levels, four mitigations Every byte drawn as it lands An invented machine, no real instruction set Nothing is uploaded Level 1/4 Mitigations none Score 0 Best — Level 1. Take the wheel 2. Kept on this device: nothing yet Reset this game’s data What the four levels are for One mitigation per level, in the order they arrived Level one is the bug on its own: an eight-cell buffer, a copy with no bound, and the saved return address two cells above it. Level two puts a random value between the two and checks it before returning, so the naive payload aborts — and then hands you an over-read that prints the value, because a canary you can read is a formality. Level three marks the stack no-execute, so returning into your own bytes faults before one of them runs, and the only targets left are routines already in the program: one to set a register, one to check it, threaded together by two addresses on the stack. Level four moves the code to a fresh base every run, so the address you have been typing since level one is a guess — and the answer is to write half of it and leave the half you cannot know alone. The leak is the hinge, and it is the same leak twice Both the canary level and the ASLR level tu Is this x86 or ARM? Will anything here work on a real program? Why can I not put a zero byte in the message? Do I have to do the levels in order? Is anything stored or sent? Neither, and not any other real instruction set. The machine is invented so that the whole of it fits beside the stack it is scribbling on: thirty-two cells, a couple of registers, and about a dozen instruction names that exist nowhere else. The shape of the frame is the honest part; the syntax is not meant to be. No, and it is not built so that it could. There is no shellcode in the game and no way to author any, the addresses are fictional, and the machine only ever enters a routine at its first instruction. What you take away is the mental model — where the return address sits, why a canary stops one case and not another, what NX changed about the shape of an exploit — and that model is worth having whichever side of it you are on. Because the copy stops at one, the way a C string copy does. It is a real constraint rather than a rule invented for the puzzle: an address containing a zero byte cannot be carried through a copy that terminates on zero, and that single fact has decided real exploits. The stack here sits on page 0x0100 so that the addresses you need do not contain one. No. The dropdown opens any of the four whenever you like, and each is a self-contained program with its own listing. They are written to be read in order, because level two only makes sense once level one has worked and level four is level three with the address taken away. pages.b: Packet Routing — Route It, Then Break It Packet routing Seven routers, eight links, and packets that have to get across. Nothing about the path is drawn in advance: each router holds its own table, every table is produced by an algorithm that can only see what a real router would see, and each hop is decided by whatever the table at that hop happens to say at that instant — including when what it says is wrong. Cut one link with distance vector running and you can watch two routers point at each other and count to sixteen while the packets between them go round in a circle until their hop count runs out. Distance vector is Bellman-Ford the way RIP does it: a router knows its own links and whatever its neighbours claim, it sends its whole vector every two seconds, and a report from its current next hop is believed even when it is worse than what it had. Link state is Dijkstra the way OSPF does it: each router floods a description of its own neighbourhood, ends up holding the who Which protocol should I pick to pass a scenario?
