Link state, on every one of them, and the reason is worth watching rather than being told: it converges in a flood plus one computation, where distance vector has to pass a metric round the network a round at a time. Static routing passes the first scenario and fails the link cut outright, because it cannot heal — it will keep posting packets into the hole until you move the next hop yourself, which you can, one router at a time. Because the count has to terminate, and it terminates by arriving at a number both ends agree means unreachable. RIP picked 16, and the price of that choice is that no network more than fifteen hops across can be served by the protocol at all. It is a ceiling on the diameter bought to put a floor under the failure. You repaired the ring. Split horizon stops a router advertising a route back to the neighbour it learned that route from, which removes the loop between two adjacent routers and nothing larger. With a ring in the map the stale route simply travels the long way round, and every router on the way adds a link cost to it. pages.t: Plasma — The Demoscene Colour Field
pages.d: A demoscene plasma built the old way: a sine table, a 256-colour palette LUT and cycling by index offset. Change the terms, the frequency and the resolution.
pages.b: Plasma — The Demoscene Colour Field Plasma Sines added together and the sum read through a colour table — one across, one down, one along the diagonal, and two measured outward from a point you can drag. That is all of it. Nothing here is a gas or a fluid or a field being simulated; the name came from the look. Every value comes out of a 2048-entry table rather than Math.sin , and the colours move because an offset into the palette moves, which is exactly how it was done when the palette was hardware. A sine table, not Math.sin Two to five sine terms Palette cycling as an index offset Renders smaller, scales up Rendering at 640 × 440 Sine terms 4 Palette cycle 0.60 turns/s Frames — Sine terms 2 sines 3 sines 4 sines 5 sines Frequency Cycle Palette Fire Ice Rainbow Greyscale Two-tone Resolution Full size Half size Third size Quarter size Pause Restart ⛶ The Plasma playfield. The game draws here once it starts. New best Ready? 0 Play Play again Resume ← → ↑ ↓ Move the field origin Drag Move the field origin Space Put the origin back in the middle Esc Pause Drag anywhere on the field to move its origin — every term is measured from that point, so the whole picture follows your finger. A tap on its own does nothing, so a stray thumb cannot move anything. The toolbar holds the number of sine terms, their frequency, the palette, the cycling speed and the resolution, and the HUD prints the size actually being filled. Kept on this device: nothing yet Reset this game’s data What a plasma actually is Interference, not physics A plasma is several periodic functions added together and the sum mapped through a colour table. There are five of them here: a sine across x, one down y, one along the diagonal, and two radial terms measured outward from the origin — the second from a centre orbiting it, which is what stops the rings looking like a target. Where crests agree you get a bright blob, where they disagree you get a dark one, and because each term drifts at its own rate the arrangement never quite repeats. Nothing about it models a gas or a fluid. The name is about the look, and the sliders are there so you can take it apart: drop to two terms and the crossed sines are plainly visible. It looks expensive and costs one lookup This is why the effect was everywhere in the demoscene. At full size the field is 640 by 440, so four terms is 1,126,400 sine evaluations a frame, or just under 68 million a second at sixty frames. Math.sin is a real transcendental call, and ask Is this a real plasma? Why a sine table when Math.sin exists? Why does it look soft at low resolution? Does it flash, and does it store anything? No, and nothing here simulates one. It is interference between periodic functions — sines added up and read through a colour table. The name is inherited from the demoscene, where it described the look rather than the physics. Because of how many times it is called. Four terms over 281,600 pixels is 1.1 million evaluations a frame, and a table lookup is an integer add, a mask and an array read where a trigonometric call is a great deal more than that. The frame counter in the HUD is there so you can watch the effect of the resolution control on your own machine rather than take my word for the arithmetic. Because the small buffer is scaled up with the browser’s own smoothing rather than as hard squares. A plasma has no edges in it to preserve, so the blur costs nothing and is close to what a CRT did to a 320 by 200 mode anyway. The HUD says which size is really being filled. The palette cycle is a continuous gradient rather than a switch between states, and if your system asks for reduced motion the toy opens on a still frame and starts the cycle slow, saying so on the screen. Nothing is stored for this page: there is no score to keep. The sound toggle is shared with the rest of the games and is the one setting that survives a reload.

This one looks one unit under your feet instead. The jump forgives two kinds of near miss Walking off a ledge leaves the jump legal for another 90 ms, and a jump pressed up to 120 ms before you land is held and fired on touchdown. Both cover presses that were real and simply fell in the frames either side of contact. Neither makes a jump longer; they only stop the game from throwing away an input it received. pages.t: Race Condition Puzzle — Break The Lock
pages.d: You are the scheduler. Interleave the threads by hand to force a lost update, a double charge, a deadlock — then meet the one lock you cannot break.
pages.b: Race Condition Puzzle — Break The Lock Race condition Every level here asks you for a wrong answer. Make the counter read 1 after two increments. Take 150 out of an account holding 100. Charge one card three times for one order. The threads are drawn as columns of numbered steps and you click one to run a single step of it, so nothing is timed and nothing is random — because a race condition is not caused by speed, it is caused by an ordering being legal. Speed only decides how often you meet it. Four of the ten levels hand you a mutex and dare you to break it anyway, and the last one is a lock used correctly, which you cannot break at all. Ten levels, nine of them breakable Every ordering counted, not estimated One level you genuinely cannot beat Nothing is uploaded Level 1/10 Score 0 Runs 0 Best 0 Step back Run it again Hint Pause Restart ⛶ New best Ready? 0 Play Play again Resume Click Run one step of that thread ← → Move between the threads Enter Run one step of the highlighted thread Space The same, and it moves the verdict on Esc Pause — there is no clock to stop Tap a thread column to run its next step. A column marked blocked is waiting on a lock somebody else holds and will not move until they release it, so tapping it only tells you who is in the way. Step back undoes one step, Run it again resets the level from the top, and Hint points at a thread that still leads to the bug. Kept on this device: nothing yet Reset this game’s data Why the bug is the objective Because finding the interleaving is the skill A demo that shows you a race condition teaches you what one looks like. Being made to hunt for the ordering yourself teaches the habit that actually catches them, which is reading a read-modify-write and asking what happens if the other thread runs here , at every line, including the ones between the lines you wrote. Every level names a specific wrong answer as the goal, so you cannot finish one by accident and you always know what you were looking for. The orderings are counted for real, and the number is not a failure rate Solve a level and the game walks its entire state space and tells you how many of the legal orderings produce the bug: 18 of 20 on the counter, 2 of 44 on the double-checked lock, 0 of 2 on the last one. That is an exhaustive search run in your tab, not a figure somebody typed in — the Hint button uses the same walk, which is how it can say whether the bug is still reachable from where you are standing. But 90 per cent of or Do I need to know threads to play this? Is the model a real CPU? Where do the ordering counts come from? Can I get stuck? How is the score worked out? Does anything leave the browser? No. Every step is one line of ordinary-looking code and the shared state is drawn above the columns as it changes, so you can work out what a level does by pressing things. What you will need by level six is the idea that a lock is a period of time rather than a spell cast over a variable, and the levels teach that by breaking four of them. No, and the page would rather say so than pretend. One step here is atomic; on a real processor an increment is several instructions and a store can be torn. Memory reordering is not simulated either — it appears exactly once, in the double-checked locking level, drawn openly as the order the compiler emitted, because inventing a plausible-looking memory model would be making something up. What is real is the interleaving, which is where these bugs actually live. A depth-first walk of the whole state space, memoised on the state, run in your browser at the moment you solve the level. Nothing is stored in the page as a lookup table. The three-request level has 33,078 legal orderings and 32,100 of them charge the card three times; the last level has two orderings and neither one is wrong. A run can reach a point where the bug is no longer reachable — that is not a bug in the game, it is the same thing as a scheduler having already made the decision for you. Step back undoes one step at a time, Run it again resets the level, and Hint will tell you either which

pages.d: The BSD rain screensaver rebuilt in a terminal grid. Drops fall, land, and throw out concentric rings that widen and fade. Density and speed controls.
pages.b: Rain — The BSD Screensaver, With Ripples That Spread Rain The screensaver that shipped with BSD games drew a dot, then an o, then an O, all in one spot, and called it a raindrop. This one lets the drop land and spread: rings in box-drawing and punctuation that widen, thin out and dissolve. Nothing about a ring is stored anywhere — every cell of it is worked out from the radius, every frame. Rings computed, not stored Four densities Round on 2:1 cells No score, no clock Falling 0 Ripples 0 Density Drizzle Steady Heavy Downpour Speed Slow Normal Fast Pause Restart ⛶ The Rain playfield. The game draws here once it starts. New best Ready? 0 Play Play again Resume This one is 78 columns wide — turn your phone sideways and it gets a great deal easier to read. Nothing to do. Watch it, or change the density and watch it harder. Kept on this device: nothing yet Reset this game’s data How the ripples are drawn A ripple is a centre and a number The obvious way to animate a spreading ring is to keep the cells it has lit and age them. That costs memory per ripple and per cell, and where two ripples overlap you then have to decide which one owns the cell as they fade. Here a ripple is a position and a radius, the radius grows with time, and the cells are derived from it fresh on every frame by walking the angle. A ripple is one small object; drawing one costs about one write per cell it actually touches. That is why Downpour can put two hundred of them on screen and the frame rate does not notice. A round ring is an ellipse in cells A character cell here is 8 units wide and 16 tall. Plot an honest circle in cell coordinates and it arrives on screen as a tall oval. Every vertical offset is halved, so the ring is an ellipse in the grid and a circle to look at. The glyph comes from the tangent At the left and right edges of a ring the curve runs vertically, so those cells get │. At the top and bottom it runs flat, so they get ─. The diagonals lean, and get / or \. Choosing the character from the direction out of the centre rather than from the direction the curve travels is an easy mistake and turns every ring inside out. Fading in four steps A terminal has no alpha channel, so the fade is four colour bands — white, cyan, blue, then dim — with the leading edge always one band brighter than the two rings trailing it. The dim band is also drawn at half density, in a fixed alternating pattern rather than a random one: random dropout would make a ring flicker every frame inste Is this the same rain that comes with Linux? Why is it silent? Is there anything to do? Why 78 columns and not 80? It is the same idea. The BSD games version animates three characters in place; this adds the spreading rings, a landing drop, and controls for how hard it rains. At the Downpour setting there are forty landings a second. A plink on each one stops being rain and starts being a fault alarm. No. It is a screensaver, which is why it sits under toys rather than games. There is no score and nothing is saved. Ripples near the edge get clipped, and two columns of margin means the widest of them still reads as a ring rather than as a stray bracket.

It is the shortest one found, not the shortest one possible, and several levels have answers that ignore the technique the level is named after entirely. Beating par is the interesting part, and nothing here believes you cannot. A golfed pattern is not a validator The email level falls to \w@\w , five characters, and that pattern would be useless against a real address. That is the honest lesson of the whole game: a pattern tuned to eight strings tells you about those eight strings. Regular expressions that have to survive input you have not seen are a different job, and usually a longer one. Why a pattern can be refused Two guards. The first reads your pattern for one unbounded repeat inside another — (a+)+ and its relatives — and refuses it before running it. The second times the tests and blacklists anything that ran long. The second one only fires after the damage: JavaScript cannot cancel a regular expression once the engine is inside it, which is precisely what makes a ReDoS a denial of service rather than a slow query. Where the backtracking actually happens The engine tries one way of splitting the input, fails, comes back and tries the next. With nested repeats there are exponentially many splittings, and it will try all of them before it admits there is no match. The regex engine lab steps through that one move at a time, which is a good deal more convincing than a paragraph about it. Questions people ask Which flavour of regular expression is this? Monsters follow you once they have seen you, the stairs only ever go down, and there is no save file — when you die you start again on level one with sixteen hit points and a dagger. Action rests a turn, or takes the stairs. ▲ ◀ ▶ ▼ Action Kept on this device: nothing yet Reset this game’s data How the dungeon is dug, and how much of it you get to see Nine cells, nine rooms, and no retries The map is split into a three-by-three grid and one room is dug in each cell, then room centres are joined. Because every room is linked to its neighbour by construction, there is no generate-and-check loop and no possibility of a level with the stairs walled off — which is the failure mode of every dungeon generator that scatters rooms at random and hopes. This one is about a person: a voice that gets annoyed when you check, a courier at the goods door at ten to five on a Friday, a message saying somebody you trust has already approved it. Each reply is scored twice — did the asset stay protected, and was the answer professionally acceptable — because those two disagree constantly, and a defender who refuses everything is the same failure as a firewall that drops everything. Each edges in, takes the quarter of the box directly ahead of it, and then finds the next quarter already held by the car on its right — who is waiting on the car in front of them . Nobody can reverse, so nobody moves again. That is not bad driving. It is a deadlock, with all four textbook conditions satisfied at once, drawn to scale in tarmac. What it costs is that green arrives on a timer rather than on demand, so push one arrival slider to the top and drag the green time down, and that arm starves while the light is busy serving an empty one. How do I make it deadlock on purpose? Which strategy is actually best? Mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption, and circular wait. All four have to hold at the same instant for a deadlock, which is why the panel shows them as four separate lights rather than as one warning — deny any single one and the entire failure becomes impossible. The Deny hold-and-wait button does that to the second one, and Clear the jam does it to the third. Leave it on Uncontrolled and tap each of the four arms in turn, which sends a car down all four at once. Otherwise just wait: at the default arrival rates the junction locks itself somewhere inside the first minute, every time, and each jam is counted. None of them, which is the point. The four-way stop is perfectly fair and pushes about half the traffic of the others, because it serialises the whole box to one car. The lights and the roundabout are close at an even load; the lights lose when the load is uneven, because they keep giving green to an empty arm, and the roundabout loses when contention is heavy, because a rolled-back car did work that produced nothing. Uncontrolled looks quickest for about a minute and then spends a third to a half of its time gridlocked — deny hold-and-wait and it becomes as fast as anything here, which is the real lesson.

A klingon you wound and then warp away from is whole again when you come back, which sounds like a bug and is the rule that makes running away expensive. pages.b: Which Cyberattack Are You — A Joke Quiz With Real Answers Which cyberattack are you A joke quiz delivered with a straight face. Fourteen questions about parties, locked rooms and comments boxes, and one of eight attacks at the end — and underneath the joke, two or three true sentences about how that attack actually works and what actually defends against it. The questions measure nothing. The paragraph is the point. Fourteen questions Eight possible attacks The result text is accurate Nothing is uploaded Progress 1/14 Pause Restart ⛶ New best Ready? 0 Play Play again Resume ↑ ↓ Move between answers Space Choose Tap an answer to move on. What the result carries is a short, accurate account of the attack you landed on: the mechanism that makes it work, and the specific thing that stops it — parameterised queries for SQL injection, validated TLS for a man-in-the-middle, tested offline backups for ransomware. Phishing and social engineering deliberately share points Every other pair of results here is separate, but phishing is social engineering — the subset that arrives in writing. Four answers score both, because a quiz that treats them as rivals teaches a taxonomy that falls apart the first time you read a real incident report. The same answers always give the same attack Ties are broken by a fixed order rather than at random, so two people who answer identically get the same result, and so do you on a second run. A joke that changes its mind on reload just looks broken. Questions people ask Does this tell me anything about myself? No. Not a thing. Fourteen questions about imaginary parties cannot measure a person, and there is no sense in which somebody resembles a denial-of-service attack. Each one says how the attack works and what actually defends against it, and none of them recommend the folk remedies — filtering rude words does not stop SQL injection, and antivirus does not stop credential stuffing. The full hash and the password itself never leave the tab, and the comparison is done locally after the response arrives. Because that is the protocol Have I Been Pwned defines, and it is not being relied on for security here — it is an index into a public dataset. Nothing is being protected by the hash; the privacy comes from only sending part of it. It asks the server to pad the response with decoy entries so every reply is a similar size. Without it, someone watching your encrypted traffic could infer which prefix you asked for from the response length alone. That is your call, and the design is what makes it defensible rather than any assurance from me. It is almost always explained in prose. Here it is drawn: a real downward-growing stack, a fixed buffer at the bottom, and a string copied into it one byte at a time — climbing straight up over the saved frame pointer and into the return address the CPU will jump to. What an overflow actually overwrites The geometry is the whole bug The stack grows downward, so a function’s local buffer sits at the bottom of its frame — and the saved frame pointer and return address sit just above it. A string copied into the buffer is written upward, toward those saved registers, with nothing in between but the absence of a bounds check. Copy one byte too many and you are writing over the address the CPU will return to. Overwriting the return address is taking the wheel When a function finishes, RET pops the saved return address into the instruction pointer and the CPU jumps there. Overwrite those four bytes and you choose the destination. Point them back at the buffer — where the attacker’s own bytes were just copied in as “data” — and the machine executes them as code. Nothing here really runs; it is a diagram of that hijack over an array in a sandboxed tab. A canary is a tripwire, not a wall A stack canary is a known value placed between the buffer and the saved registers, checked just before the function returns. A linear overflow has to run through it to reach the return address, so the check fails and the program aborts. What the four panes are showing Tokens are the easy part The lexer walks the text once, left to right, with a single character of lookahead and no idea what a program is. It cannot tell you that print print is nonsense, because deciding that is not its job — it will hand over two perfectly good keyword tokens and let the next stage refuse them. Almost every “unexpected token” message you have ever seen comes from the stage after this one. The tree is where precedence lives There is no precedence table anywhere in the parser. What is actually happening AES is four moves, repeated Substitute every byte through the S-box, rotate the rows, mix the columns, XOR in the round key — then do it nine more times. This tool reverses them for you and shows the gap between each pair — a large gap means the message sat in a queue or a filter, and a negative one means the chain was forged or the clocks disagree. What SPF, DKIM and DMARC each prove SPF says the sending server was authorised to send for that domain. DKIM says the message is cryptographically signed and unmodified. DMARC says the domain owner accepts the combination. All three passing proves the message really came from that domain — not that it is honest. A lookalike domain registered yesterday passes all three too. The Reply-To mismatch A From: line showing a familiar name and a Reply-To on a different domain is the standard setup for business email compromise. The recipient sees the trusted name, and their reply goes to the attacker. This is flagged in red. Why nothing is looked up A WHOIS query, a geolocation call or a reputation check all tell a third party which address you are investigating, and in a targeted case that leaks the investigation itself. The originating IP is extracted and shown; what you do with it is your call. Questions people ask Where do I find the raw headers? Authentication proves origin, not honesty. The ones added by servers you trust cannot, but a sender can inject fake ones before the message reaches those servers. Only the hops added after the message entered infrastructure you trust are reliable, which is why the timing checks matter. If the first hop shows a 10.x, 192.168.x or 172.16-31.x address, the message started inside a private network and the public IP appears at the next hop out.

pages.b: HTTP Version Race — 1.1 vs 2 vs 3 HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2 and HTTP/3, raced on the same link Almost every explanation of these three protocols describes the differences. Very few show them, and the distance between “HTTP/3 handles packet loss better” and watching HTTP/2 freeze solid while HTTP/3 keeps running is the whole distance between a claim and an understanding. So this lab loads the same page three times at once, over one link whose latency, bandwidth and packet loss you set, and draws the three waterfalls side by side. What each version actually changed HTTP/1.1: one request at a time, per connection A connection carries one request and waits for the whole response before the next one can go. Browsers worked around that by opening six connections per origin, so the seventh resource waits for a lane to free up regardless of how fast the link is. Pipelining was supposed to fix it and did not: middleboxes reordered or mangled the responses, so browsers shipped it disabled and eventually removed it. Sites shipped domain sharding instead — serving assets from img1, img2, img3 purely to buy more connections. HTTP/2: one connection, many streams — and one queue underneath HTTP/2 put every request on one connection as an independent stream, interleaved frame by frame, and compressed the headers with HPACK so the repeated ones stop costing anything. Six lanes became one lane carrying everything. What it did not change is what is underneath: a single TCP connection is a single ordered byte stream, so the streams are independent to the application and not independent at all to the transport. HTTP/3: the streams moved below the ordering QUIC is a new transport on top of UDP, and Is this a real network connection? Why does HTTP/2 fall apart when I raise the loss slider? Move a slider and the three runs are recomputed from scratch; that is all it is doing. Because HTTP/2 multiplexed its streams on top of a single TCP connection, and TCP delivers one ordered byte stream. When a segment goes missing, TCP will not hand the application anything that comes after the hole - not for the stream that lost the packet, and not for the fifteen that did not. So one lost packet freezes every stream until the retransmit arrives. That is TCP head-of-line blocking, it cannot be fixed above the transport, and it is the entire reason HTTP/3 exists. No, and this lab will show you that if you look. On a clean link HTTP/3 is ahead by about one round trip of handshake and very little else. Under loss it is clearly better than HTTP/2, but it is not immune: QUIC runs congestion control too, so a lost packet still cuts its sending window. UDP is also deprioritised or blocked outright on some networks, and QUIC does more work in userspace, which costs CPU. It is a real improvement, not magic. It is the shortest decimal that no other double is closer to, chosen by the printing routine. The value is 0.3000000000000000444089209850062616169452667236328125, exactly, with nothing left over — every binary fraction terminates in decimal, because one half is five tenths. pages.t: JWT Decoder & Verifier — Offline and Safe
pages.d: Decode and verify JSON Web Tokens in your browser. Reads the header and payload, explains every claim, checks expiry and verifies HMAC signatures.
pages.b: JWT Decoder & Verifier — Offline and Safe JWT decoder and verifier A JWT is a bearer credential: whoever holds it can act as that user until it expires. Pasting a production token into a website hands that credential to whoever runs the site. This one has no server behind it — check the Network tab and see for yourself. Header, payload and claims explained Expiry and not-before checks HMAC signature verification Warns on alg: none Token never transmitted Before you start This tool runs entirely inside your browser. Nothing you paste or drop here is uploaded, logged or stored — which for security work is the whole point, not a footnote. What it does not do No uploads — there is no server to upload to No account, no history, nothing saved Large files are capped so the page stays responsive No lookups against any external database Why that matters here Evidence files stay on your machine A token or key you paste is never transmitted Nothing you paste ever appears in your Network tab Works with no internet once the page is cached Free, permanently I understand — open the tool Take me home ▶ Run ⛶ HMAC secret Token JWT Output What a JWT actually guarantees Decoding is not verifying The payload of a JWT is base64url, not encryption. Anyone holding the token can read every claim in it, which is why you must never put a secret in one. Only the signature says whether the claims were tampered with, and checking it needs the key. The alg: none attack The header names the algorithm, and the header is attacker-controlled. A library that trusts it will happily accept {"alg":"none"} with an empty signature, letting anyone mint a token for any user. This tool flags it in red. Real servers should pin the expected algorithm rather than reading it from the token. Expiry is the only revocation JWTs are stateless, which means there is usually no way to revoke one before it expires. A token with no exp claim is valid forever. Short lifetimes plus a refresh token is the standard answer. Why this one is local The advice never to paste a production token into a website is correct, and awkward, because the well-known decoders are websites. This is the same tool without that problem: the token is split and verified with WebCrypto in your tab. Questions people ask Is my token sent anywhere? No. The token is decoded and verified in your browser using the built-in WebCrypto API. There is no server in this tool and no network request carries the token - open the Network tab in developer Is my token sent anywhere? Can it verify RS256 or ES256 tokens? Why does it say my token is expired when the app still works? Is a JWT encrypted? What should I do if I pasted a real token into another site? No. The token is decoded and verified in your browser using the built-in WebCrypto API. There is no server in this tool and no network request carries the token - open the Network tab in developer tools and you will see nothing. Signature verification here covers HS256, HS384 and HS512, which use a shared secret. RS and ES algorithms are verified with a public key rather than a secret; the token is still fully decoded and all claims are checked, but the signature is not. Expiry is compared against your device clock. If your clock is wrong, so is the answer. Servers also commonly allow a small amount of clock skew. No. A standard JWT is signed, not encrypted, and its payload is readable by anyone holding it. If you need the contents hidden, that is JWE, which is a different thing. Treat it as compromised and invalidate the session. Anything with a long expiry and no revocation path is worth rotating.

pages.t: What Your Browser Leaks — IP, GPU, Canvas
pages.h: What your browser tells every website
pages.d: See what any site learns about you without asking: public and local IP via WebRTC, your GPU, time zone, and a canvas fingerprint that survives clearing cookies.
pages.b: What Your Browser Leaks — IP, GPU, Canvas What your browser tells every website None of this needed a permission prompt. Every number below was read the moment you opened the page, and any site you visit can read the same. Your public IP, via WebRTC Your address on your own network GPU, time zone, cores, screen A fingerprint that survives clearing cookies None of it reaches this site — though finding your public IP means asking a STUN server, so Google and Cloudflare see it ⛶ Your addresses A page can open a WebRTC connection to nobody, collect the addresses the browser offers, and read them straight out. No prompt, no warning. It is how VPN leak checkers work. The one thing it cannot do alone is learn your public address: that answer comes from a STUN server, so this page asks Google’s and Cloudflare’s the moment it loads, and they see your IP in the asking. Gathering … asking a STUN server what address you appear to come from Your browser and machine Which of these actually matter Most single values here are harmless. Your screen size tells nobody anything. The problem is that they combine: screen, time zone, language, GPU, core count and font rendering together are usually enough to pick one browser out of millions, and none of it is stored in a cookie you can clear. The canvas fingerprint is the sharpest one. The same drawing instructions produce microscopically different pixels depending on your GPU, driver and font stack. Hash those pixels and you get a number that stays the same across visits, survives private browsing in many cases, and has nothing to do with cookies at all. The public IP address is the one people are usually surprised by, because they assume a VPN hides it. It often does. But WebRTC asks a STUN server directly, and if that request escapes the tunnel, the address you see above is your real one rather than the VPN’s. If those two differ, your VPN is leaking. If your local address shows as a random name Something like a3f9c1d2-….local instead of 192.168.1.14 means your browser is doing its job. Chrome and Firefox now hide the real local address behind a random mDNS name unless the site already has camera or microphone permission. The public address is not hidden that way, and cannot be — it is how packets find their way back. What to do about it Use a browser that resists fingerprinting if it genuinely matters to you — Tor Browser makes everyone look identical, which is the only real defence. If you use a VPN, check the public addres Does any of this reach your server? Why is my public address missing? I use a VPN. Should the public address be the VPN one? Why is my local address a random name ending in .local? Does clearing cookies change the canvas fingerprint? No. Every value in the table is computed in your tab and thrown away when you close it, and this page stores nothing of its own. Its one request is the WebRTC probe, which asks the Google and Cloudflare STUN servers what address you appear to come from — there is no way to learn a public address without showing it to somebody. Analytics loads here as on every page of this site, so Google does receive the ordinary pageview signals: browser, screen size, language, and a location derived from your address. Several of those are rows in the table above, which on this page of all pages is worth saying plainly. Gathering finished without one, usually because a firewall is dropping UDP; the five-second timer is only the outer bound. If WebRTC is switched off in your browser altogether, the row reads unavailable rather than going blank. Extensions that merely restrict which addresses WebRTC may use often still let the public one through, so a blank here is the stronger signal. Yes. Compare the address above against whatever address your VPN provider says it is giving you. If they differ, the WebRTC request escaped the tunnel and every site you visit can read your real address the same way this page just did. That is what a VPN leak is. Replacing the last bit of each changes the colour by at most one step, which is far below what an eye or a screen can resolve. Three bits per pixel means a one-megapixel image carries about 375 KB. It survives nothing Re-save the image as JPEG, resize it, or upload it anywhere that re-encodes images, and the message is gone — because all of those rewrite exactly the bits it lives in. Steganography hides the existence of a message; cryptography protects its contents. If the content matters, encrypt it before hiding it. pages.d: Step through the TCP handshake with real sequence numbers, walk both endpoints through the state machine, and watch Reno congestion draw its sawtooth.
pages.b: TCP Visualiser — Handshake & Congestion TCP, from handshake to sawtooth The pcap analyser elsewhere in Labs shows you TCP packets after they have flown. This lab runs the protocol. Watch the three-way handshake exchange real sequence numbers, watch both ends walk the TCP state machine to ESTABLISHED and back, and watch congestion control probe for bandwidth and back off on loss — the sawtooth that shapes very nearly every byte you have ever downloaded. The three-way handshake with real seq / ack numbers Both endpoints through the TCP state machine Reno congestion control, actually simulated Slow start, fast recovery and timeout, distinct Change the loss pattern and watch the shape respond Before you start This runs entirely inside your browser — the animation, the maths, all of it on your own machine. Nothing is uploaded and there is no server. Good to know Everything runs on your device Heavy work runs off the main thread where it can Nothing is uploaded or stored Why it is here Seeing it beats reading about it Works offline once the page is cached Free, permanently I understand — start Take me home ⛶ Starting the TCP visualiser… if this message stays, it did not load — please tell me, and mention your browser. What TCP is doing under a download The handshake is a sequence-number agreement SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK is not a greeting ritual — it is both ends agreeing on the sequence number each will start counting from, so that every byte afterwards can be ordered and acknowledged. A SYN consumes one sequence number; data advances it by its length; an acknowledgement is always “the next byte I expect from you”. The numbers on the ladder are the real arithmetic, not decoration. TIME_WAIT is the state everyone forgets Closing a connection takes four segments, not three, because each direction is shut independently. The side that closes first then sits in TIME_WAIT for twice the maximum segment lifetime — long enough that a straggling old segment cannot be mistaken for part of a new connection reusing the same ports. It is why a busy server can accumulate thousands of sockets in TIME_WAIT, and why that is normal rather than alarming. Congestion control is why the internet works at all No sender knows how much bandwidth the path has, so TCP finds out by probing: start slow, double the window every round trip until something is lost, then back off and probe more gently. Because every connection does this, they share a link roughly fairly without any central coordinator Are the sequence numbers real? Which congestion-control algorithm is this? Why does the window collapse to 1 on a timeout but only halve on duplicate ACKs? Is this a real network connection? Is anything uploaded? Yes. The handshake tracks genuine seq/ack arithmetic - a SYN or FIN consumes one sequence number, data advances the sequence by its length, and each acknowledgement is the next byte expected. The test suite checks these against the worked examples in RFC 793. TCP Reno: slow start, congestion avoidance, fast retransmit and fast recovery. It is the classic textbook algorithm and the ancestor of what most systems still run. Modern variants like CUBIC and BBR change the growth curve, but the core idea - probe up, back off on loss - is the one shown here. Because they signal different things. Duplicate ACKs mean packets are still arriving, so the path is working and a gentle cut is enough. A timeout means the sender has heard nothing back, so it must assume the pipe has drained and start probing from scratch. That asymmetry is deliberate and is the shape of the sawtooth. No. It is a simulation of the protocol running as arithmetic in your browser. Nothing is sent, no socket is opened, and the only real TCP involved is the one that delivered this page. They are all “a number”, and reading one with the wrong epoch puts your event in 1601. So this reads it under all of them. Windows counts 100-nanosecond ticks from 1601, because that is the start of the Gregorian 400-year cycle. Apple counts from 2001 in Cocoa and from 1904 in HFS+. None of them are wrong; they just do not interoperate. Where you meet each one FILETIME comes out of the registry, NTFS MFT records and Windows event logs. WebKit microseconds come out of Chrome’s History, Cookies and Login Data databases. Cocoa comes out of macOS and iOS plists. Getting these wrong puts an event centuries away from where it belongs, which is a common and embarrassing timeline error. The identification trick Because the epochs are so far apart, reading one number under all of them almost always leaves exactly one answer in a believable date range. That single plausible reading tells you which system wrote it, without knowing anything else about the source. MS-DOS timestamps inside ZIPs A packed 32-bit value with the date in the high half and the time in the low half, at two-second resolution — which is why file times inside a ZIP archive are always even. Both sides can compute the handshake traffic secrets the instant ServerHello lands, because the key shares and the transcript are all they need — so EncryptedExtensions, the certificate, CertificateVerify and Finished are all already encrypted. Every row in the ladder carries the key it travels under, taken from the model rather than drawn on, so the two versions cannot quietly disagree with each other. pages.b: Free Word Cloud Generator — Shapes & PNG Word cloud generator Paste an essay, a speech, a set of reviews or a whole book chapter, and watch the words that matter rise to the top — sized by how often they appear, packed into a shape, coloured to taste, and yours to download as a PNG. How it makes the picture Size means frequency The one thing a word cloud communicates is which words appear most: the biggest word is the most common one. So the text is counted — each word’s size comes from how often it occurs — and the ordinary filler words (“the”, “and”, “of”) that appear in every text are dropped, because they would dominate the cloud while saying nothing about your text in particular. You can turn that off, or add your own words to ignore. Packed by pixels, largest first A word is placed where none of its own inked pixels touch a pixel already used — not where its rectangle happens to be free. That is the difference between words that sit in a grid of boxes and words that tuck into the bowl of a big letter. The biggest words go down first and take the middle; then the list is cycled again at steadily smaller sizes, down to a few pixels tall, and it is that tail of small words that reaches into a heart’s cleft or a star’s points and makes the shape actually read. The shape is a stencil, not a crop Pick a heart, a teddy bear or a rocket and the words are only placed where they fit inside that outline — the cloud grows into the shape rather than being drawn as a rectangle and then clipped. pages.b: Krunalkumar Shah Research | Publications & Ideas Research interests Exploring ideas that connect technology, security, and thoughtful innovation. Research remains central to my work, whether it is publishing academic material or applying fresh thinking to cybersecurity and practical systems. Publication Security Against Fork Bomb Attack in Linux Based Systems Krunalkumar D. Shah & Krunal V. Patel · International Journal of Research in Advent Technology (IJRAT), Vol. 7, No. 4, April 2019 · E-ISSN 2321-9637 · DOI: 10.32622/ijrat.74201911 🏅 Nominated for the Best Paper Award in Linux research at IAENG The problem I set out to solve A fork bomb is a denial-of-service attack in which a process endlessly replicates itself until the process table and memory are exhausted, freezing the system. What drew me to it is that creating a process is a legitimate operation needing no special privileges, so even hardened Linux systems are vulnerable — availability, one of the three pillars of information security, breaks down. Why the existing defenses weren’t enough Static process limits reject legitimate work once the cap is hit. Rate limits misfire on fork-heavy software such as CAD tools. Name-based blacklists never forgive: a legitimate process that shares a name with a past offender is killed forever. Each approach trades one failure mode for another, and that is the gap I set out to close. The defense I proposed I combined name-based detection with something I call process resource quarantine. New processes are monitored for their fork rate; offenders are killed and their name recorded. When a recorded name reappears, I do not kill it outright — it runs inside a resource quarantine and is inspected. If it behaves, it is released and removed from the list, so a false positive corrects itself instead of lasting forever. What my results showed I evaluated the system with a bash fork bomb on Xubuntu 18.04 (kernel 4.15). It identified an attack in as little as 44 ms at a threshold of 500 forks, while known offenders were handled instantly by name — and the machine stayed responsive and available throughout, which was the whole point.
